lessons.plain: Experimenting early means trying a small, working version of an idea before committing to the full build. A thin increment is the smallest slice of a product that is real enough to test with actual users, so you learn whether people want it and whether the approach works. The second half concerns the team's surroundings: an environment that rewards learning treats a disproven idea as useful information rather than a failure to hide. Teams that do this find problems while they are still cheap to fix. Think of it as a short rehearsal before the full production, where a flop costs far less.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has spent four months building a full reporting module, and nobody has yet checked whether customers would use it. What is the cheapest way to find out whether it is worth finishing, and what would you do if the answer were no?
lessons.teach:
A hypothesis is a clear, testable guess about what users or the market will do, such as 'dispatchers will open the alert at least three times per shift.' A thin increment is the smallest working piece of the product that can test that guess. It is not a half-finished product; it is a deliberate experiment with a narrow scope, a fixed time limit, and a measure that will show whether the guess was right. Validated learning is the knowledge gained from comparing what happened with what you predicted. It works because real behaviour is far more reliable than opinion, and a small test exposes wrong assumptions before the expensive work begins.

Worked example. A delivery team wants a route-alert feature for dispatchers. Step 1: write the hypothesis, that five dispatchers will read at least one alert per shift for two weeks. Step 2: build the thin increment, a single alert type for one depot, delivered by a simple script and a shared message channel, with no new screens. Step 3: run it for two weeks. Step 4: measure. Three dispatchers used alerts daily, and two said they wanted the alert on the map rather than in a message channel. Step 5: decide. The team changes the next increment to a map alert instead of building the full feature set.

A common mistake is polishing the thin increment until it looks like the finished product, which consumes the time the experiment was meant to save. Another is hiding a disproven idea because the team is judged only on shipped features. Where that happens, teams keep building the full feature, discover the problem in production, and ship the wrong thing at higher cost.

An environment that rewards learning is one where a clear negative result is celebrated as a cheap lesson, so the team reports it openly.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic group wants to know whether text reminders will reduce missed appointments. The team writes this hypothesis: at least 60 percent of patients who receive a reminder text will confirm their appointment within 24 hours. For the thin increment, a receptionist sends texts by hand from a spreadsheet to 80 patients at one clinic, with no new software. The test runs for three weeks. At the end, 41 of the 80 patients (about 51 percent) confirmed within 24 hours, against the predicted 60 percent. Step 5, the decision step, is still blank. Which completion is correct?
choices: Report the 51 percent result openly as a validated lesson, record that the prediction was missed, and change the next thin increment (for example, testing a different send time) rather than building the full system.
Rebuild the spreadsheet process as a branded app screen so that the next test looks more professional before anyone measures again.
Keep the test running for another month without reporting the 51 percent figure, so the team does not appear to have missed its own target.
Build the automated reminder system for all clinics now, because a result near 50 percent shows the idea is mostly right and the gap is small enough to ignore.
questions.why: The decision step uses the measured result to change the next small experiment and reports the miss openly, which is how validated learning is supposed to work, while the other choices either overbuild, hide the result, or polish the increment.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the best example of a testable hypothesis in the sense used for a thin increment?
choices: Users will find the premium export feature valuable and enjoy using it.
We should build a full export module with PDF, CSV and Excel formats because competitors offer them.
At least 15 percent of free accounts that click the export button will start a 14-day paid trial within the next six weeks.
Export is an important feature that the product roadmap should include in the next major release.
questions.why: A testable hypothesis names a group, a behaviour, a number and a time limit so the result can be checked against what was predicted.

questions.prompt: A team ran a thin increment, got a clear negative result, and the manager responded by lowering the lead's performance rating. In the next quarter, the team stops reporting disproven ideas. What is the most likely consequence for the running product?
choices: The product will be safer, because fewer people will argue about the results of experiments.
The team will complete the experiments faster, because the reporting step has been removed.
The team will switch to larger, longer experiments so that single negative results carry less weight.
The team will keep building features that have already been disproven and find the problems late, when fixing them costs more.
questions.why: When negative results are hidden, the team keeps building the disproven idea and discovers the problem after release, when the cost of fixing it is higher.

questions.prompt: A bank wants to test whether small-business customers will use a pre-approval check for loans. The team has six people and three weeks. Which option is the best thin increment for this test?
choices: A manual pre-approval form sent by email to 20 small-business customers, with a fixed two-week window and a measure of how many complete it.
A survey of the bank's branch managers asking whether they think small businesses would want pre-approval.
A complete loan origination module with account management, document upload and credit scoring, built before any customers are asked.
A redesigned mobile app home screen with the pre-approval feature placed in the navigation, released to all customers at once.
questions.why: A thin increment is a narrow, time-limited experiment with a measure that shows whether the guess was right, and the manual form with 20 customers and a completion count fits that description.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a thin increment is and how it helps a team decide whether to keep building a feature. Name one limit or tradeoff of experimenting this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: A thin increment is the smallest working slice of a feature that can test one specific assumption, such as whether users will actually use it. We build it with a clear hypothesis and a short time limit, then measure what people do rather than what they say. That lets us stop or redirect a feature before the full cost is spent. The main limit is that a small test can mislead. A few users, a short window, or a narrow depot can produce a result that does not hold at scale, so we have to state the sample size and conditions and treat the result as a reason for the next test, not as proof. A second tradeoff is cultural. If the team is judged only on shipped features, people will hide negative results, so the experiment only works if leaders treat a clear disproof as a useful outcome.
rubricPoints: Defines a thin increment as the smallest working slice that tests one assumption
Explains that the experiment needs a clear, measurable hypothesis and a time limit
States that the result guides the next decision: continue, change, or stop
Names a limit, such as small samples misleading the result, or a culture that hides failures

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises this, and reasoning through a team scenario about choosing an experiment adds the most to the explanation.

lessons.plain: This is about looking at a piece of work and asking how predictable it is before deciding how to run it. Some work is like following a recipe: the steps are known and the result repeats. Some work is like building a bridge from a known design: harder, but experts can plan it in advance. Some work, like a busy market or a product whose users will react in ways nobody has seen, is unpredictable, so you learn what works by trying small things and watching the results. An agile mindset means matching how you plan and check progress to the kind of work you face, instead of using one process for everything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A checkout bug shows up for some customers only, and each fix the team tries either does nothing or breaks something else. Should the team write a detailed plan for the whole fix before touching code, or run small changes and watch what happens? Why?
lessons.teach:
Complexity classification is a way of sorting a situation by how well cause and effect can be known before you act. Three tools are named in this objective. Cynefin is a framework with domains. In the clear domain, cause and effect are obvious and you apply best practice. In the complicated domain, experts can work out cause and effect through analysis, so you apply good practice. In the complex domain, cause and effect only become clear in hindsight, so you probe, sense, and respond. In the chaotic domain there is no clear cause, so you act first to stabilize. The Stacey Matrix plots two things: how much people agree on the outcome, and how certain they are about how to reach it. Where the work lands on that grid points to a similar zone. A complex adaptive system is a set of many interacting parts, such as users, services, and teams, whose combined behavior emerges from their interactions and cannot be predicted from any single part.

Why it works: in complex work, a detailed up-front plan rests on guesses about reactions that have not happened yet. Short experiments produce evidence sooner, so the plan can change.

Worked example: a team is asked to make a dispatcher screen feel faster, with no agreed measure of faster and unknown causes. Step 1: is the outcome agreed? No. Step 2: is the route to it known? No, because the slowness varies by user and load. That places the work in the complex domain. Step 3: choose a fitting practice, such as trying two or three small, safe-to-fail changes behind a switch, measuring each one, and reviewing the results at the next retrospective.

Common mistake: classifying by team preference rather than by the situation, or treating a complicated problem as complex and skipping the expert analysis that would have answered it.

Consequence: if a complex problem is run as a fixed plan, the team reports progress against tasks while users stay unhappy, and the gap appears late.

Match the practice to the domain. Do not apply one process to everything.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union's accounts team wants fewer customer complaints about duplicate fee charges. Step 1: is the outcome agreed? Yes, the team and the branch managers both agree that duplicate charges should drop to near zero. Step 2: is the route to it known? Yes, the charges come from one specific rule that pairs fee events with account batches, and the rule can be read and tested directly. Step 3 is missing. Name the domain this places the work in and the practice that fits it.
choices: Complicated domain: have an expert analyze the batching rule and apply the good practice that analysis supports
Clear domain: apply the best practice the credit union already uses for every fee type
Chaotic domain: act first to stabilize by freezing all fee charges until the complaints stop
Complex domain: run three or four small safe-to-fail changes behind a switch and review them at the retrospective
questions.why: Agreed outcome and a known but non-obvious route place the work in the complicated domain, where expert analysis of cause and effect is the fitting practice.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a complex adaptive system as the course defines it?
choices: A set of many interacting parts, such as users, services, and teams, whose combined behavior emerges from their interactions and cannot be predicted from any one part
A single component whose behavior can be fully predicted by reading its specification
A group of experts who agree on a plan and then follow it without revision
A fixed sequence of steps where each step's output is the next step's only input
questions.why: The course defines a complex adaptive system as many interacting parts whose combined behavior emerges and cannot be predicted from any single part.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain's app team agrees that a new loyalty feature should increase repeat visits, but no one can say which feature design will do it, and the team cannot name the causes of low repeat visits. What should the team do first?
choices: Write a complete feature specification covering all rewards and send it to the bakery managers for sign-off
Ask the managers to vote on the loyalty reward and build whichever option gets the most votes
Hire an outside consultant to produce a single definitive model of customer visit behavior
Probe with a few small, safe-to-fail experiments behind a switch, measure each one, and review the results
questions.why: Agreed outcome with unknown route and unclear causes places the work in the complex domain, where the course says to probe, sense, and respond with small experiments.

questions.prompt: A ride-share company's team builds a 40-page fixed plan for a rider rating feature. Every task is reported green each sprint, yet rider complaints rise. What is the most likely underlying mistake?
choices: The team ran complex work as a fixed plan built on guesses about user reactions that had not happened yet
The team should have assigned more testers to the feature so the complaints would be caught earlier
The team classified the work as chaotic and should have stabilized it with a hotfix
The team reported progress and should have reported it in story points instead of tasks
questions.why: A detailed up-front plan in complex work rests on guesses about reactions not yet seen, so task progress can look fine while users stay unhappy and the gap surfaces late.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a piece of work should be planned in detail up front or handled through short experiments, and name one limit or tradeoff of your classification method.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking two questions: do we agree on what the outcome should be, and do we know how to get there? If both answers are yes, the work is closer to complicated or clear, so a detailed plan and expert analysis make sense. If the outcome is agreed but the route is unclear, or the outcome itself is contested, the work is complex, so I would run a few small, safe-to-fail experiments, measure them, and adjust at the next review. The main limit is that the classification is a judgment made with incomplete information, so a team can misjudge the domain. That is why I would revisit the classification after each experiment, rather than treating the first answer as permanent. Another tradeoff is that experiments take time to show results, so the team has to accept slower visible progress in exchange for learning sooner.
rubricPoints: Decides the domain by asking whether the outcome is agreed and whether the path is known
Links complex work to small experiments and frequent review rather than a fixed up-front plan
Names a limit such as misjudging the domain or slower visible progress
Notes that the classification should be revisited as new evidence arrives

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style team scenario to classify its complexity and pick a fitting practice adds the most here, since no listed mission or planned engine targets this skill directly.

lessons.plain: This is about helping a group of people work as one team on purpose. A team vision is a short, shared statement of what the team is trying to achieve and why it matters. Working agreements are simple promises the team makes to itself about how it will work together, such as how quickly it answers questions or how it handles disagreement. A high-performing team is one where people trust each other, raise problems early, and get work done without constant supervision. A retrospective is a regular meeting where the team looks back at recent work and chooses one or two changes to try next. Together these habits turn a collection of individuals into a team that keeps getting better.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new team of six people has never worked together. In the first week, which would help them more: a long list of rules handed down by a manager, or a short set of agreements the team writes itself? Why do you think so?
lessons.teach:
A team vision is a short statement, shared by everyone on the team, of the outcome the team is aiming for and why it matters to the people it serves. A working agreement is a small set of norms the team writes itself, such as how quickly it responds to questions, how it runs its meetings, or how it handles work that is blocked. A high-performing team is a group where members trust one another, raise problems early, and make decisions without waiting for a manager to approve each step. A retrospective is a recurring meeting, usually held at the end of each sprint (a fixed-length work period, often two weeks), in which the team reviews how it worked, identifies what to keep, and picks a small number of changes to try next.

Why this works: people commit to what they helped create. A vision the whole team wrote gives members a reason to choose between competing priorities, and agreements the team wrote are easier for peers to uphold than rules imposed from outside. Retrospectives turn experience into improvement, because each small change is tested in real work and then reviewed again at the next meeting.

Worked example: a five-person team building a customer portal notices that code reviews keep arriving late and bugs slip into releases. Step one: the team restates its vision as customer changes reach users safely every week. Step two: at the retrospective, members observe that reviews wait until the end of the sprint. Step three: they agree on a working agreement that every change gets a review within one working day. Step four: the next retrospective checks whether the agreement held and whether bugs dropped. The change is kept or dropped based on that evidence.

Common mistake: treating the vision as a poster on the wall and the agreements as a policy document nobody revisits. Retrospective actions that are never followed up make the meeting feel like a complaint session and erode trust.

Consequence in a running system: a team that skips retrospectives keeps repeating the same release failures, while a team that acts on them shortens the time between a problem appearing and a fix reaching production. Improvement comes from the habit of inspecting and adjusting, not from good intentions.

questions.prompt: A four-person claims team at a regional insurer maintains a form-processing tool. Step one: the team restates its vision as every claimant hears a decision on a submitted form within five working days. Step two: at the retrospective, members notice that forms wait on one person's validation check, and that person is often away. Step three: the team writes a working agreement that any form waiting for validation is checked by a second member within one working day. Steps one to three are done. Which step is still missing before the team can decide whether to keep or drop the agreement?
choices: Ask the team manager to approve the agreement at the next sprint planning meeting
Add a second validation check to every form so that waiting disappears entirely
Write the agreement into the company's vendor contract so it cannot be changed later
At the next retrospective, check whether forms were validated within one working day and whether waiting times fell, then keep or drop the change
questions.why: The retrospective cycle ends with checking the agreement against evidence at the next meeting, then keeping or dropping the change based on that evidence.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a working agreement as the term is used in agile teams?
choices: A statement of the outcome the team wants, shared with its stakeholders and customers
A signed policy that managers use to measure each individual's performance
A list of bugs to fix in the next release
A short set of norms the team writes itself, such as response times or how it handles blocked work
questions.why: A working agreement is a small set of norms the team writes itself, so the other options describe a vision, a management policy, or a backlog.

questions.prompt: A product team of six holds a retrospective every sprint and records four changes each time, but nobody checks those changes at the next meeting. What is the most likely result?
choices: The team's vision gets rewritten automatically at the start of each sprint
Velocity doubles within two sprints since changes stop being tracked
Members gain time for deep work because meetings shrink in length
Retrospectives start to feel like complaint sessions, and trust wears down
questions.why: Retrospective actions that are never followed up make the meeting feel like a complaint session and erode trust, so the correct option names that consequence.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour most clearly marks a high-performing team, as opposed to a team that waits for approval?
choices: The team keeps one shared calendar for all tasks
Members avoid conflict so that meetings stay short
The manager signs off every task before work starts
Members raise problems early and decide small steps themselves
questions.why: A high-performing team raises problems early and makes decisions without waiting for a manager to approve each step, which the last option describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined a newly formed team how a team vision, working agreements and retrospectives work together to build a high-performing team. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on working agreements.
lessons.modelAnswer: The vision tells us where we are heading, so people can make consistent choices without asking permission for every one. Working agreements turn that into concrete habits, such as how we respond to blockers, so we do not renegotiate the basics every week. Retrospectives are where we check whether those habits actually work and change the ones that do not. Together they build trust, because people see the team keeping its promises and improving them. One limit is that agreements only help if the team follows them, and they can harden into rigid rules that stop the team adapting. So we review them at each retrospective and treat them as current best guesses, not permanent law. Another tradeoff is time: retrospectives and agreement-making take hours away from delivery, and a team that skips them saves time now but repeats the same failures later.
rubricPoints: A team vision is a shared outcome that guides choices, written by the team rather than imposed.
Working agreements are concrete team norms that peers can hold each other to.
Retrospectives inspect how the team works and turn findings into small changes that are tested and reviewed.
Trust and high performance come from the team keeping its promises and improving them over time.
A limit is named, such as agreements becoming rigid or retrospectives costing delivery time, with a way to manage it.

suggested.rationale: Explaining how vision, agreements and retrospectives fit together to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed mission has the learner do it.

lessons.plain: Transparency in agile work means that everyone on the team, and people outside it who depend on the work, can see how the work is really going without having to ask. An information radiator is a display of that picture, such as a physical board, a shared wall chart, or a live online dashboard, that the team keeps current as work moves. It shows progress, known risks, and anything blocking the team, so problems surface early instead of hiding in someone's inbox. The same idea applies whether people sit in one room or across several time zones. The display and the communication habits just have to be chosen differently.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team lead learns that a dependency on another department has blocked two developers for three days, yet nobody mentioned it at the daily check-in. Without any reading, what is the most likely reason this stayed hidden, and what single change to how the team shows its work would have surfaced it the same morning?
lessons.teach:
An information radiator is any display of team status placed where people pass by it, kept up to date by the team, so that people can learn the state of the work without a meeting. Transparency is the broader goal: making progress, risks, and impediments visible to everyone who needs them. An impediment is anything that stops or slows a team member from finishing work, often called a blocker. A risk is an uncertain future event that could harm the work if it happens. Co-located means the team works in the same place; distributed means it is spread across locations or time zones.

It works because people notice what sits in front of them, and a visible blocker reaches the people who can clear it, who would otherwise never hear about it. The gap between a problem appearing and someone acting on it gets shorter.

Worked example. The team board has columns for To Do, Doing and Done, plus a Blocked area and a short risk list. Step 1: Priya moves her card to Blocked and writes the reason: waiting on a security review requested Monday. Step 2: The whole team and the product owner can see the card at a glance. Step 3: At the daily check-in nobody has to ask. The product owner sees the review has been pending three days and calls the security team. Step 4: By afternoon the review is done and the card returns to Doing.

Common mistake: treating the radiator as a report that one person updates once a week, or quietly leaving out items that look bad. The display then shows a comfortable picture while the real blockers live in private chat threads.

For distributed teams the radiator becomes a shared online board, paired with a short written update and a fixed window of overlapping hours for live conversation. The content stays the same; only the medium changes. Transparency is judged by whether a problem becomes visible to people who can help within a day, not by how polished the display looks.

questions.prompt: A billing team of six sits in one office. Their board has To Do, Doing, Done, a Blocked area and a short risk list. A risk is an uncertain future event that could harm the work if it happens. Step 1: Ana writes a risk card: the software vendor may not deliver the new invoice module by 14 March. Step 2: The card sits on the board where the team and the supplier liaison see it at the Monday stand-up. Step 3: [missing step] Step 4: On Thursday the liaison confirms the module will arrive 21 March, and the team re-plans its work around that date. Which action fills the missing Step 3?
choices: Ana deletes the risk card because nothing has gone wrong yet.
The team waits until 14 March to see whether the risk actually happens.
The liaison calls the vendor on Tuesday and the team records the firm date on the risk list.
Ana emails a weekly summary to the sponsor only and leaves the board unchanged.
questions.why: The risk must be acted on within a day so people who can help see the problem early, and a call to the vendor followed by recording the answer on the board is what Step 4 depends on.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an impediment, as the course defines the term?
choices: The project may overrun its budget if the vendor raises prices.
A teammate is on leave next week and will be away for five days.
A server might fail sometime next month and cause an outage.
A developer cannot finish a story today because the test environment is down.
questions.why: An impediment is anything stopping or slowing a team member from finishing work now, while the other items are uncertain future events (risks) or future absences that have not yet blocked work.

questions.prompt: A five-person team keeps its Blocked column empty for weeks, yet people keep saying they are stuck. Blockers get discussed only in a private chat thread. What is the most likely cause, and the right fix?
choices: The sponsor is reading the board too often, so the team should show it to the sponsor only once a month.
The team has no risks, so it should delete the risk list and rely on the daily stand-up.
The board is too small, so the team should add more columns for every stage of the work.
The team is quietly leaving out blockers that look bad, so the team should move each blocker onto the visible board with a reason as soon as it appears.
questions.why: Leaving out items that look bad is the common mistake that makes the radiator show a comfortable picture while real blockers stay hidden, so the fix is to make every blocker visible to the people who can clear it.

questions.prompt: A team has members in two cities with only three hours of overlapping working time each day. Which communication setup best matches the course's approach for distributed teams?
choices: Each person keeps a private status document that they share only when a manager asks for it.
Daily phone call with the product owner, held at whatever time suits the caller.
Weekly PDF report emailed to the manager after each review, read whenever convenient by anyone who wants it.
Shared online board, short written update, fixed overlap hours
questions.why: For distributed teams the course pairs a shared online board with a short written update and a fixed window of overlapping hours for live conversation, keeping the same content while changing only the medium.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to agile how an information radiator helps a team split across two time zones, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on shared displays instead of meetings.
lessons.modelAnswer: An information radiator is a shared display, here an online board, that the team keeps current with its work, blockers and risks. For a team split across two time zones, it means someone in the other zone can see what happened overnight without waiting for a reply, and a blocker logged in the morning is visible before the other half starts. It replaces a lot of status meetings that would otherwise need everyone online at the same hour. The limit is that a display only shows what people choose to put on it, so it can look reassuring while real problems stay in private messages. It also goes stale quickly if nobody owns updating it. That is why I would pair the board with a short written update and a fixed overlap window for live talk when something needs a real conversation.
rubricPoints: Defines an information radiator as a shared, team-maintained display of status, risks and blockers
Explains that visibility lets someone in another time zone see progress and blockers without waiting for a reply
Names a real limit, such as displays being incomplete, going stale, or hiding problems that stay in private chats
Notes that distributed teams still need live overlap time or written updates to handle items that need conversation

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how visibility and communication habits work across co-located and distributed teams, and no listed mission makes the learner practise that.

lessons.plain: Psychological safety means people on a team feel safe to speak up, admit mistakes, ask questions, and disagree without fear of being punished, embarrassed, or ignored. In a project manager's job, this is something you build on purpose. You do it by treating mistakes as a learning topic rather than a hunt for someone to blame, by steering conversations toward dialogue where people explore options together instead of trying to win, and by welcoming people who question how things are always done. Teams that feel safe surface problems early, when they are still cheap to fix.
lessons.guessPrompt: A release went wrong and the team meeting goes quiet, with two people staring at the table. What do you think a project manager should do in the next ten minutes to make it likely that the real cause gets named?
lessons.teach: Psychological safety is a shared belief within a team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks: to admit a mistake, ask a question that might look ignorant, or challenge a plan. It is a property of the group, not of one person's personality. In agile work it matters because complex product work depends on people reporting bad news early, and fear of blame is the most reliable way to hide that news. Three practices carry most of the weight. First, a no-blame culture: when something fails, the review asks what in the system allowed it and what the team will change, not who should be punished. Second, dialogue over debate: in debate people defend positions to win, while in dialogue they explore assumptions together to understand the problem better. A facilitator can ask what would have to be true for each option to work. Third, normalizing challenges to the status quo: the project manager explicitly invites people to question why something is done, and thanks them when they do, so challenging the process is ordinary rather than disloyal. Worked example: a sprint ends with a missed commitment. Step one, the manager states the facts without judgement: three of eight stories were not done. Step two, the manager asks each person for their view of what slowed the work, starting with the newest member so they speak before a senior engineer anchors the room. Step three, the team records one system change, such as splitting stories smaller, and checks next sprint whether it helped. Common mistake: believing safety means being nice. A manager who says great effort to everyone while ignoring the real gap teaches the team that problems are not discussed. Safety includes candor. Consequence: when safety is low in a running delivery team, impediments stay hidden until they cause an outage or a missed date, which costs far more to fix than an uncomfortable conversation would have. Psychological safety is built through repeated small behaviors, not one announcement.

questions.prompt: A payments team at a different company ships a currency rounding change. Two days later, QA engineer Priya reports that she had noticed the change had no tests but stayed quiet because she did not want to look like she was slowing the release. The delivery lead responds in this order. First, he thanks Priya for raising it and states the facts without judgement: the change shipped with zero rounding tests and two customer invoices were off by a cent. Second, he asks the group what would have to be true for the release to be safe, and he hears from the newest developer first. Third, the step that completes his response is missing. Which choice fills that third step?
choices: He agrees one system change, such as a rounding test in the release checklist, and checks at the next release whether it helped.
He holds off all further releases until the team has agreed, in writing, on who should have caught the missing test and what consequences follow.
He asks Priya to write a formal statement of her hesitation so the reason for the delay is on record before any review takes place.
He names the developer who wrote the rounding change so the team knows who owns the mistake going forward.
questions.why: After the facts are stated and views are heard, the no-blame approach records one system change and checks whether it helped, rather than assigning a person or stalling work.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's operations team asks anyone who reports a late shipment why they did not fix it sooner. Which statement best describes psychological safety as the teaching text defines it?
choices: A shared belief in the group that it is safe to admit mistakes, ask questions, or challenge a plan.
A manager's policy that every mistake is followed by a written apology from the person involved, filed with human resources.
A personality trait where some people are naturally calm enough to take risks in front of others, so the team does not need to do anything.
A rule that the team avoids discussing problems in public so that meetings stay calm and nobody feels uncomfortable.
questions.why: The teaching text defines psychological safety as a shared belief within the group about taking interpersonal risks, not as a personality trait or a rule about apologies or silence.

questions.prompt: A payments team's deployment fails. The team lead asks in front of everyone who skipped the regression test. Which response best matches the no-blame practice?
choices: Ask what in the process let the test be skipped and what the team will change.
Ask the group who skipped the test, but do it privately so the person is not embarrassed in front of their peers during the review.
Ask the group to agree that whoever skipped the test should lose release rights for the next month as a clear consequence.
Accept that a test was skipped and move on without discussing it, since the release has already been rolled back and fixed.
questions.why: A no-blame review asks what in the system allowed the failure and what the team will change, rather than who should be punished, even if the question is asked privately.

questions.prompt: Two engineers on a supply-chain software team argue for opposite database designs, and each defends their own design to win. The facilitator then asks what would have to be true for each design to work. What is the facilitator doing?
choices: Settling the argument by choosing the design the more senior engineer prefers, so that the team can move on quickly.
Postponing the decision until the next sprint so that the debate has time to cool down before anyone reconsiders their stance.
Asking the team to vote anonymously on the design so that no one is exposed to challenge from peers and the decision is made quickly.
Shifting the group from defending positions toward exploring the assumptions behind each option, which is dialogue rather than debate.
questions.why: Dialogue explores assumptions together to understand the problem, and asking what would have to be true for each option is the facilitator move the teaching text describes for that purpose.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who thinks psychological safety just means being nice: what it is, how a project manager builds it in practice, and one limit or tradeoff of pushing for it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Psychological safety is a team belief that people can speak up, admit mistakes, and disagree without being punished or humiliated. It is not niceness. A team can be very friendly and still hide problems. As the project manager, I build it through three habits. I keep reviews focused on system causes rather than individuals, so mistakes become data. I shift disagreements from debate toward dialogue by asking what would need to be true for each option to work. And I invite challenges to how we work, thanking people who push back. The tradeoff is time: open discussion takes longer than a quick decision by the most senior person, and it can slow a team under a hard deadline. I accept that cost for complex work, where hidden problems cost far more later, but for simple, well understood work I would decide faster.
rubricPoints: Defines psychological safety as a shared team belief about taking interpersonal risks, not mere friendliness
Names at least two concrete practices: no-blame reviews, dialogue over debate, or inviting challenges to the status quo
Explains that safety is needed so problems surface early in complex work
States a real limit or tradeoff, such as slower decisions or time cost under deadline pressure

suggested.rationale: Explaining the idea back to a teammate, including its tradeoffs, is the core skill here and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: A feedback loop is the cycle of building something, showing it to people, and learning from their reaction. The shorter the loop, the sooner a team finds out it is heading the wrong way, while changing course is still cheap. Shortening the loop has two parts: bringing the right people, especially those who will use or pay for the result, into the work from the first day, and using quick ways to test ideas, such as sketches, rough prototypes or small releases, instead of building for months in private. It is like a cook who tastes the soup while cooking rather than serving a full pot at the end.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team spends four months building a reporting feature in private, then shows it to the customer for the first time. The customer says it does not answer their real question. Would it have been cheaper to learn this in week one or in month four, and why?
lessons.teach:
A feedback loop is the cycle of making something, getting a reaction from the people it is for, and changing the next step based on what you learned. Its length is the time between a decision and the moment you find out whether that decision was right. A stakeholder is anyone affected by the work or able to accept, reject or fund it, such as a user, a sponsor or an operations manager. Involving stakeholders from day one means they shape the problem and see early versions, not only the finished product.

Two named approaches help shorten the loop. Design thinking is a set of human-centred steps (understand the user, define the problem, generate ideas, prototype, test) that moves quickly from listening to a cheap test. Lean startup describes a build-measure-learn cycle in which a team releases a minimum viable product, the smallest version that can test a key assumption, and measures real behaviour before building more.

Worked example: a dispatch team wants a route-suggestion feature. Step 1: in week one they talk to two dispatchers and learn the real problem is re-planning after delays, not initial routing. Step 2: they sketch a paper screen and walk a dispatcher through it, which takes an hour. Step 3: they build a minimum version that only proposes a revised route for one delayed vehicle, release it to two dispatchers, and watch whether they use it. Within two weeks the loop has run several times, and the team knows whether the idea deserves more effort.

Common mistake: treating a single end-of-project demo as stakeholder involvement. A demo that arrives after months of building gives a long loop, however friendly the audience.

Consequence in a running system: a feature built in isolation can reach production carrying assumptions nobody has checked, so the first real signal is often an incident or a spike in support requests.

Shorter loops make being wrong cheap, and cheap mistakes are how a team learns fastest.

questions.prompt: A call-centre team at a regional bank wants a script-suggestion tool for its agents. Step 1: in week one they sit with four agents and learn the real pain is finding the right fee explanation mid-call, not writing the opening greeting. Step 2: they print a one-page mock-up and walk one agent through two sample calls in under an hour. Step 3 is missing from this record. Step 4: after two weeks of use, they check whether agents still open the old policy wiki during calls. Which choice fills the missing Step 3?
choices: Spend three months building the full tool, then release it to all 300 agents at once.
Write a training manual for agents so they can use the tool correctly once it ships.
Ask the bank's operations director to approve a budget before anyone builds anything.
Build a narrow version that only suggests the fee explanation, release it to one team of agents, and count how often they use it during calls.
questions.why: Step 3 is the smallest working release that tests the key assumption with real users, which is what gives Step 4 something real to check, so the narrow release to one team is the missing step.

questions.prompt: In the teaching text, which description best defines a stakeholder?
choices: Any person who reads the project status report once a month.
Only the developers who write and test the code for the product.
Anyone affected by the work or able to accept, reject or fund it, such as a user, a sponsor or an operations manager.
The single executive who signs the final invoice when the project closes.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a stakeholder as anyone affected by the work or able to accept, reject or fund it, with users, sponsors and operations managers as examples.

questions.prompt: An insurance claims portal team plans to show its first working version to stakeholders only at go-live, nine months after starting. Which problem does this plan create, according to the teaching text?
choices: The team cannot use design thinking steps because they have no prototype at all.
The loop between a decision and learning whether it was right becomes about nine months long, so wrong assumptions surface late.
The stakeholders will receive too much documentation at once to read.
The sponsor will be legally required to approve every feature before testing.
questions.why: A single late demo stretches the loop, which is the time between a decision and finding out whether it was right, so mistakes are found late and become expensive.

questions.prompt: A small nonprofit with a tight budget wants to know whether volunteers will actually use a new shift-sign-up feature before spending money on the full version. Which approach from the teaching text fits best?
choices: Release a minimum viable product that tests the key assumption, then measure real behaviour before building more.
Run a large annual survey and build whatever the majority of respondents describe.
Delay all releases until the feature is complete so the first test is fully polished.
Write a complete requirements document and get it signed by every board member before building.
questions.why: Lean startup uses a minimum viable product, the smallest version that tests a key assumption, and measures real behaviour before investing further, which suits a tight budget.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is skeptical of talking to users all the time why shortening the feedback loop matters, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would say a feedback loop is how long it takes from making a choice to learning whether that choice was right. If we only show stakeholders finished work, we can spend months building the wrong thing, and fixing it then is expensive. Shortening the loop means involving the people who use or fund the work from the start, and testing small versions quickly, such as a sketch or a minimal release, to check our assumptions. The tradeoff is that frequent involvement costs stakeholder time and can pull the team in many directions. So we need to choose which people and which questions matter most for each loop, and not treat every opinion as a requirement.
rubricPoints: Defines a feedback loop as the time between a decision and learning whether it was right.
Explains that stakeholders should be involved from the start, not only at the end.
Names a quick testing technique such as a prototype, sketch or minimum viable product.
States a real limit or tradeoff, such as stakeholder time or conflicting opinions.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the loop and its tradeoffs back to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Embracing change means expecting that what people want from a product will shift as the team learns, and treating that shift as useful information rather than a failure. Imagine planning a road trip and then discovering the bridge is closed: a good driver reroutes instead of insisting on the original map. In agile work, the team keeps its wanted features in one ordered list, reorders it when something new is learned, and checks each change against the goal they are working toward. The aim is to deliver the most valuable thing possible, not the plan that was written first.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is halfway through a two-week sprint and a customer asks to change a feature they have already seen working. Before any teaching, what do you think the team should do first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Embracing change means accepting that requirements and priorities will move, and building a way to respond that protects the product rather than the original plan. A requirement is a need the product must meet. A priority is the order in which the team works on those needs. In agile work, requirements are kept in a product backlog, an ordered list maintained by the product owner, the person who decides what the product should do next. A sprint is a fixed length of time, commonly two to four weeks, during which the team works toward a single sprint goal.

Why this works: the team learns most after it builds something real and people use it. If the plan were frozen at the start, the team would keep delivering what was true last month. Shorter loops let the team inspect results and adapt the next step.

Worked example. A dispatch team is two days into a sprint building a map filter. Their sprint goal is filtering vehicles by depot. On day three, the operations lead says filtering by vehicle type is now more urgent because of a new contract. Step 1: the product owner judges the value of the new request against the current goal. Step 2: the team estimates its size. Step 3: if it fits without breaking the sprint goal, the product owner swaps it in for a lower-priority item of similar size; otherwise it goes to the top of the backlog for the next planning session. The team does not silently absorb it.

Common mistake: treating every change as an emergency, so the sprint goal is abandoned and nothing gets finished. Consequence: work is half-done everywhere, nothing reaches users, and the team has no trustworthy evidence about what to build next.

Changing the product is a normal, managed part of the work, and a team that reorders honestly delivers more value than one that protects its first plan.

questions.prompt: A hospital ward scheduling team is four days into a two-week sprint whose goal is showing live bed counts for each ward. The nursing director then asks for a discharge-time forecast, which the team estimates at 13 points, more than any item already in the sprint and enough to threaten the sprint goal. Step 1: the product owner compares the forecast's value with the current goal and judges it important but not urgent this week. Step 2: the team's estimate of 13 points is recorded. Step 3: because the forecast would break the sprint goal, the product owner [blank]. Which completion correctly finishes Step 3?
choices: places the forecast at the top of the product backlog for the next planning session and leaves the sprint goal unchanged
adds the forecast to the sprint and extends the sprint by one week without telling the nursing director
cancels the bed-count goal so the team can start a new sprint goal built around the forecast
asks the team to absorb the forecast silently and finish both items by working extra hours
questions.why: When a change would break the sprint goal, the product owner moves it to the top of the backlog for the next planning session rather than changing the current sprint.

questions.prompt: In agile product work, which term names the order in which the team works on the needs the product must meet?
choices: requirement
sprint goal
priority
sprint
questions.why: A priority is the order of work on needs, while a requirement is the need itself, so the order is the priority.

questions.prompt: A payments team of five is mid-sprint when a stakeholder asks for a fraud-flag change of roughly the same size as an item already in the sprint, and the change does not threaten the sprint goal. Which response best follows the adapt-by-reordering approach?
choices: The team abandons the sprint goal and restarts planning so the new request fits cleanly.
The team waits until the sprint review to mention the request so the current sprint is not disturbed.
The product owner swaps the fraud-flag change in for a lower-priority item of similar size, and the sprint goal stays intact.
The team quietly adds the fraud-flag change on top of its current work and keeps every existing item.
questions.why: When a similar-sized change fits without breaking the sprint goal, the product owner swaps it in for a lower-priority item, which keeps the work honest and the goal intact.

questions.prompt: A logistics team treats every incoming change request as an emergency and drops its current sprint goal each time. What is the most likely consequence for the running system?
choices: Work is left half-done across many items, nothing reaches users, and the team lacks reliable evidence about what to build next.
Users receive more features more often, so the product improves faster than the team could plan.
The backlog shrinks on its own because urgent work replaces lower-value items automatically.
The team's velocity rises because context switching forces people to finish tasks more quickly.
questions.why: Treating every change as an emergency abandons sprint goals, which leaves work unfinished and gives the team no trustworthy evidence to guide the next step.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who worries that agile means changing direction constantly how a team should handle a shifting requirement in the middle of a sprint. Name one limit or tradeoff of accepting change.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell them agile does not mean the plan changes whenever someone has an idea. It means the team expects priorities to move because they learn from working results, and it has a set way to handle that. When a new request comes in mid-sprint, we ask the product owner how it compares in value to the current sprint goal, and we check how big it is. If it fits without breaking the goal, we swap it for something similar in size. If not, it goes to the top of the backlog for the next planning session. The tradeoff is real: every accepted change costs focus and can delay work already in progress, so we limit mid-sprint swaps and keep the sprint goal visible so everyone can see what is being given up.
rubricPoints: Change is expected because the team learns from working results, so it is not a sign of failure.
The product owner compares a new request against its value and the current sprint goal.
A change is either swapped for similar-sized work or placed in the backlog, never silently absorbed.
Accepting change costs focus and delays work in progress, so mid-sprint changes are limited.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario of a shifting priority adds the most, and no listed mission currently covers responding to change.

lessons.plain: Empowering a team means giving people the room, information and support to make good decisions themselves, rather than waiting for the leader to decide. Several habits make that work. Trust is the belief that people will keep their word and that honest mistakes will not be punished. Transparent communication means sharing the real state of the work, including bad news, early and openly. Coaching means helping someone find their own answer by asking good questions. Mentoring means passing on your experience through advice and example. Emotional intelligence is noticing feelings in yourself and others and responding calmly, so that a disagreement becomes a problem to solve rather than a fight to win.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer keeps missing sprint commitments and has stopped mentioning problems at standups. Before any teaching, what is the first thing a project manager should do, and what should they avoid doing?
lessons.teach:
Coaching means helping a person reach their own answer by asking good questions, instead of handing them the solution. Mentoring means sharing your own experience and advice with someone who wants to grow a skill. Trust is the expectation that people will keep their commitments and that honest mistakes will not be punished. Transparent communication means the real state of the work, including problems and bad news, is visible to everyone early rather than held back. Emotional intelligence is the ability to notice feelings in yourself and others and to respond to them with care rather than reacting on impulse.

Why it works: people commit to decisions they helped shape, and they raise problems early only when raising them feels safe. Trust makes that safety possible, and transparency keeps the whole team's picture of reality accurate.

Worked example: two engineers argue at standup about whether to cache results or query the database each time. Voices rise and the rest of the team goes quiet. The project manager does three things. First, she speaks to each engineer separately and asks what outcome each cares about, learning that one fears slow pages and the other fears stale data. Second, she restates the disagreement as a question both can test: which option meets both needs, and what would prove it. Third, she agrees a short timebox for a comparison spike and posts the result on the team board where everyone can see it.

Common mistake: stepping in to end the tension by declaring a winner. The quarrel stops, but the underlying concerns stay hidden, and the losing engineer stops offering ideas.

Consequence: when conflict is suppressed rather than resolved, problems move underground. Risks go unreported and blockers surface late, which is exactly when they are most expensive to fix.

questions.prompt: A delivery lead at a payments company sees one developer's estimates run late for three sprints in a row. Step 1: she meets the developer privately and asks what makes the work hard to size. The developer says requirements change partway through each sprint. Step 2: she asks the developer what would make the estimates more reliable, and the developer proposes freezing scope at sprint start and logging every mid-sprint change separately. Step 3 is missing. Which action completes the sequence?
choices: Agree a two-sprint trial of the developer's proposal and record the change count on the shared team board where everyone can see it
Move the developer to a different team so the late estimates no longer affect her own reporting
Rewrite the developer's estimates herself and send the corrected figures to the stakeholders as the official plan
Tell the developer to add a 50 percent buffer to every future estimate without discussing the reason
questions.why: The coaching approach has the person test their own idea and makes the result visible to the whole team, so the lead neither imposes an answer nor hides the evidence.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes coaching from mentoring as the course defines them?
choices: Coaching means helping someone reach their own answer through good questions, while mentoring means sharing your own experience and advice with someone who wants to grow a skill
Coaching means telling the person the answer you already know, while mentoring means letting them find the answer through their own effort
Mentoring means assigning a task to a junior member, while coaching means reviewing their finished work after it is complete
Coaching and mentoring are the same activity, and the only difference is whether the manager is paid for the time spent
questions.why: Coaching is defined by using questions so the person reaches their own answer, and mentoring is defined by sharing your own experience with someone who wants to grow.

questions.prompt: On a team at a regional bank, a developer honestly reports that a commitment slipped because of an error in their own reasoning. The team lead responds by publicly reprimanding the developer in the next meeting. What is the most likely consequence for the team's trust and communication?
choices: It speeds up delivery, because the fear of reprimand pushes everyone to finish their commitments sooner than originally planned
It has no lasting effect, because the slipped commitment was already recovered and the developer apologised
It makes the team more willing to take on large risks, because people learn they must perform well to avoid blame
It breaks the expectation that honest mistakes are not punished, so future problems are likely to be hidden
questions.why: Trust is the expectation that honest mistakes will not be punished, so punishing one undermines that expectation and makes people less likely to surface problems early.

questions.prompt: At a retail firm, a project manager ends a dispute between two engineers about a database index by immediately choosing one engineer's option in front of the team, without first learning what concerns each engineer has. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The losing engineer becomes more creative, because being overruled motivates them to propose stronger alternatives later
The team's schedule is unaffected, because the decision was made quickly and the work continues as planned
The disagreement is fully resolved, because a clear decision removes the reason for either engineer to raise concerns again
The quarrel stops, but the underlying concerns stay hidden, the losing engineer stops offering ideas, and risks surface late
questions.why: Declaring a winner suppresses the conflict rather than resolving it, so concerns go underground and problems emerge late when they are costlier to fix.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that as a project manager you should only coach people and never tell them what to do. Explain in your own words when coaching is the right move, when mentoring is better, and one limit or tradeoff of coaching when a team is in conflict.
lessons.modelAnswer: Coaching and mentoring are both useful, but they fit different moments. Coaching works when the person already has the knowledge and needs to find their own answer, so I ask questions such as what they have tried and what would prove it. Mentoring fits when they lack experience, so I share what I have seen work and explain why. The limit of coaching is time and patience. When a team is stuck on a risk that could hurt delivery this week, a question-only approach can drag on too long. In a conflict, I would first talk to each person privately to understand their underlying need, then turn the argument into a testable question with a timebox. I should not force the answer myself, because that teaches the team to wait for me to decide.
rubricPoints: Coaching draws out the person's own answer through questions, while mentoring shares experience and advice
Choose the move based on whether the person has the knowledge or lacks the experience
A tradeoff of coaching is that it can be slow when time pressure is high
In conflict, speak to each person privately to find underlying needs before reframing the disagreement as a testable question

suggested.rationale: Telling which coaching, mentoring or conflict move a scenario calls for is best practised by reasoning through exam-style team situations, and no existing mission or planned engine covers leadership moves directly.

lessons.plain: When a team keeps running into the same kind of trouble, a facilitator's job is to work out why it happens before rushing to a fix. This objective covers two steps: digging into the underlying cause of a problem, and then choosing the response that will help the most rather than the one that is quickest to start. Think of a doctor who asks what is actually making a patient ill before prescribing something, and who weighs several treatments before picking one. In agile work this matters because a fix aimed at a symptom tends to come back.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sprint keeps ending with stories carried over, and the team's answer each time is to add more people to the next sprint. Without any further teaching, what is one better first question a facilitator could ask, and why?
lessons.teach:
A root cause is the underlying condition that, if removed, would stop a problem from recurring. A symptom is what you see on the surface. Root-cause analysis is the set of methods for moving from the symptom to the cause. Two common tools are the Five Whys, where you repeatedly ask why until you reach a cause you can act on, and the Ishikawa diagram, also called a fishbone diagram after Kaoru Ishikawa. An Ishikawa diagram puts the problem at the head of a line and draws bones for cause categories such as people, process, tools and environment. Its job is to generate candidate causes, not to name the answer. A resolution strategy is the chosen response: remove the cause, change a process, add capacity, or accept and monitor. The best strategy is the one that addresses the cause at acceptable cost and risk.

Worked example. Step 1: state the problem precisely, such as 40 percent of stories not finished in each of the last four sprints. Step 2: brainstorm causes by category. Two members are part-time on another project, stories are being added after planning starts, and the shared test environment is often booked. Step 3: ask why. Testing waits because the environment is booked by another team, and nothing sets a booking rule. Root cause: no agreed way to reserve the shared environment. Step 4: compare options. Adding people does not touch this cause and adds coordination cost. Reducing work per sprint treats the symptom. A booking rule with a trial period targets the cause cheaply. Then check the next sprints.

Common mistake: accepting the first plausible cause, or choosing the fix that is easiest to start, and treating the diagram as the answer instead of a list of candidates to test. Consequence: carryover continues, and the team stops trusting the retrospective.

A good resolution is judged by whether it removes the cause at reasonable cost, not by how quickly it can be started.

questions.prompt: A payments team reopens tickets after release in 3 of its last 5 releases. Step 1 (state the problem): 3 of 5 releases had reopened tickets. Step 2 (brainstorm by category): one developer is new to the code, the release checklist is a shared document that several people edit, the staging database is refreshed by hand from production at irregular intervals, and the team has no shared definition of done. Step 3 (ask why) is not shown. Which statement is the root cause the team should act on?
choices: Nobody owns the staging data refresh, which is done by hand at irregular intervals, so tests pass on data that no longer matches production.
The release checklist should be locked so that only one person can edit it at a time, which would prevent conflicting versions of the steps.
The team should lengthen the sprint so testing can finish before the release date, which would give reopened tickets time to be caught.
The new developer needs more time to learn the codebase before releases, so the team could pair them with a senior engineer for the next three sprints.
questions.why: The correct statement names an underlying condition with no owner that, if fixed, would stop the mismatch from recurring, while the other three either describe a person, a schedule, or a document rather than the condition behind the reopened tickets.

questions.prompt: A support desk's ticket backlog grows every Monday. Which of these is the symptom rather than the root cause?
choices: The backlog is larger on Mondays than on any other day of the week.
No one is assigned to triage weekend emails before the Monday start.
Weekend emails arrive with no category and sit unsorted until staff return.
The triage rota ends on Friday afternoon with no handover to the weekend cover.
questions.why: The Monday backlog size is what is visible on the surface, while the other three are conditions that could be removed to stop the backlog from recurring.

questions.prompt: A product team misses its sprint goals about 35 percent of the time because a shared design-review slot is often cancelled at short notice. Which resolution best fits the goal of removing the cause at reasonable cost?
choices: Stop including design-dependent stories in sprints so that the misses no longer appear on the board.
Hire a second designer to share the review load, although the cancellations would still happen.
Set a standing rule that a cancelled review moves automatically to a fixed backup slot, trial it for two sprints, then compare the miss rate.
Track the misses on a wall chart for the next sprint and discuss them at the retrospective.
questions.why: Moving cancelled reviews to a fixed backup slot targets the cause cheaply and can be checked against the miss rate, whereas the other options add capacity, hide the symptom, or only monitor without changing anything.

questions.prompt: After one fishbone session, a team decided the cause of its missed releases was a new build tool and bought extra licences. The misses continued. What was the main mistake?
choices: They were right that the tool was the cause, but they should have waited longer before judging the result.
Fishbone diagrams cannot be used for problems involving tools, so the team should have used another method.
They should have bought more licences for the whole department instead of only the team.
They accepted the first plausible candidate and treated the diagram as the answer, instead of testing each candidate cause.
questions.why: An Ishikawa diagram only generates candidate causes, so the mistake was accepting one candidate without testing it against the others, which the teaching text names as the common error.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, who thinks recurring problems are always solved by adding capacity, how you would investigate the root cause of a recurring problem and choose a resolution. Name one limit or tradeoff of the method you use.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by describing the problem with numbers, such as how many stories slip each sprint, so we agree on what we are fixing. Then I would gather candidate causes from several categories, like people, process, tools and environment, using a fishbone diagram or a group brainstorm. For each candidate I would ask why repeatedly until we reach something we can change. Only then would I compare resolutions by asking which one removes the cause at reasonable cost and risk. Adding people often fails this test because it adds coordination work without touching the cause. The limit of this approach is that the diagram only lists what the group thinks of, so a cause nobody knows about can be missed. Also, Five Whys can stop too early or follow one chain only. I would therefore run the chosen fix as a short trial and check the results in the next sprints.
rubricPoints: Defines root cause as the underlying condition, distinct from the visible symptom
Explains how an Ishikawa diagram or Five Whys generates and tests candidate causes
Compares resolution options by how well they remove the cause, not by ease of starting
Names a real limit, such as missed causes or stopping the why-chain too early

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning from a symptom to a root cause and justifying a resolution in words, which no current or planned hands-on mission directly exercises.

lessons.plain: When a project finishes, or a sprint ends, the team has learned things: what slowed them down, what worked, and what they would do differently. Most of that knowledge fades within weeks unless someone deliberately writes it down and makes it easy to find. Knowledge sharing as a project leader means setting up the habits and places where lessons get captured, and then making sure people in other teams can actually reuse them when they start similar work. The leader's job is to make this normal and safe for the team, not to write every note alone.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team finished a three-month project, and six months later a different team started a new project and made the same mistake. Why do you think that happened, and what single change would most likely have prevented it?
lessons.teach:
A lesson learned is a short, recorded insight about something that happened on a piece of work, written so someone else can use it. A good lesson has three parts: the situation, the result, and the action to take next time. Organizational knowledge is the pool of such lessons across teams and initiatives, kept in a shared place such as a lessons log or wiki. A retrospective is the regular team meeting where people inspect how the work went and agree on changes; it is the most common place lessons are created.

Why it works: knowledge only transfers when it is captured in a form that a stranger can find, understand, and judge as relevant. A bare complaint like 'the vendor was slow' helps nobody. A lesson with context and an action can be reused.

Worked example. In a payments project, the team discovered late that the vendor's test sandbox allowed only 100 calls per minute, which broke their load tests and cost two weeks. Step 1: at the sprint retrospective, the team names the issue. Step 2: they write the lesson with the situation (sandbox quota), the result (two-week delay), the action (request a production-like test quota in week one), and tags (vendor, integration, testing). Step 3: the leader files it in the shared lessons log and links it to the vendor's integration page. Step 4: six months later another team starts an integration with the same vendor, searches the tags during planning, finds the entry, and adds the quota request to its first sprint.

Common mistake: treating the lessons log as a write-only archive or a place for blame. Entries with no owner, no context, and no tags are never found. Another mistake is capturing lessons only at project closeout, when people have forgotten the details.

Consequence: without reuse, the same vendor limit surfaces again as a late failure at go-live, when fixing it is most expensive.

questions.prompt: A regional warehouse team found that their handheld barcode scanners froze after about 500 scans and needed a manual reboot, which stalled a stocktake for half a day. At the retrospective they named the problem. They wrote a lesson with the situation (scanners freeze after roughly 500 scans) and the result (a half-day stall during stocktake). The action is missing from their draft. They then filed the entry in the shared lessons log with an owner and the tags hardware and stocktake. Two months later a second warehouse starts a stocktake, searches the tag stocktake, and finds the entry. Which action completes the lesson so the second team can use it?
choices: Before the next stocktake, test each scanner's scan count and schedule a reboot before the limit.
Ask the vendor for a fix in the next budget cycle and leave the lesson open until they reply.
Reboot the scanners every hour during any stocktake, regardless of how many scans have been done.
Record that the scanners are unreliable so future teams avoid them when possible.
questions.why: A usable action is a specific step the next team can take before the problem appears, and testing scan counts and scheduling a reboot before the limit does that, while the other choices are either vague, wait on an outside party, or give no actionable step.

questions.prompt: Which three parts make up a useful lesson learned, as described in the course text?
choices: The situation, the result, and the action to take next time
Complaint, vendor name, and budget impact
Date, owner, and final cost
Team name, sprint number, and velocity
questions.why: The text defines a lesson as having a situation, a result, and an action to take next time, and the other choices list details that may be recorded but are not the three required parts.

questions.prompt: A team runs a six-week project and captures all its lessons only at closeout. By then, the developer who handled the vendor integration has left and the details are fuzzy. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Closeout memory is accurate enough, so the entries need no context.
Retrospectives become unnecessary once a closeout review exists, which saves time.
The next team cannot judge whether the lessons apply and may repeat the delay.
Filing the lessons under the project name makes them easy to find later.
questions.why: The text warns that capturing lessons only at closeout loses details, and without context a later team cannot judge relevance, so the same problem can recur.

questions.prompt: A team building a retail reporting dashboard searches the shared lessons log during planning and finds an entry: a single sign-on provider's login tokens expired during long sessions and caused repeated re-login loops; the action was to test token lifetime in the first week. What should the team do?
choices: Copy the whole lessons log into the team's own wiki so nothing is missed.
Add a token-lifetime test as an early planning item, since the entry's action applies to this provider.
Skip the search because a dashboard is a different kind of product from the original work.
Wait until the first demo to see whether token expiry happens before doing anything.
questions.why: Organisational knowledge is reused by finding a relevant entry during planning and turning its action into work, which the first choice does, while the others ignore the lesson, delay it, or copy material without applying it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is about to start a project similar to one that just ended how you would capture the lessons from the last project and make them useful to the new team. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would capture lessons during the work, at each retrospective and at major milestones, not only at the end. Each lesson gets a short write-up with the situation, the result, and a concrete action, plus tags such as vendor, technology, or process area. We store them in one shared log with a named owner for each entry. Before the new project's planning, the new team searches the tags for their topics and turns any relevant lessons into planning items or checklist entries for their first sprint. The main tradeoff is effort: writing good lessons takes time, and the log goes stale unless someone reviews it periodically and removes entries that no longer apply. A second limit is transfer: a lesson from one context, such as a different team size or vendor version, may not apply, so the new team has to judge relevance rather than copy the action blindly.
rubricPoints: Capture lessons during the work, such as at retrospectives and milestones, not only at closeout.
Record each lesson with its situation, result, and a concrete action rather than a bare complaint.
Make lessons findable through tags or a shared store, and have the new team check them during planning.
Name a real limit, such as the time cost of writing, stale entries, or lessons that do not transfer to a different context.

suggested.rationale: Explaining how lessons get captured, found, and judged for reuse in a new context is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Agile is a way of working where a team builds things in small pieces, checks real results often, and adjusts.
