The agile mindset is the set of beliefs behind that way of working: people and conversations matter more than paperwork, working results matter more than promises on paper, customers work with the team rather than only signing a contract, and change is expected rather than resisted. As a project leader, promoting it means helping people understand why these beliefs matter, not just getting them to run the meetings. Continuous improvement means a team regularly looks at how it works, picks one small change, tries it, and checks whether it helped. Together they describe a team that gets better on purpose.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has held daily standups and two-week sprints for six months, yet keeps missing its commitments and nobody talks about why. Before any teaching, what do you think is actually missing, and what would you do first as the project lead?
lessons.teach:
The agile mindset is the set of beliefs and priorities behind agile practices. It is often summarised by the four value pairs of the Agile Manifesto: individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working outcomes over heavy documentation, customer collaboration over rigid contract terms, and responding to change over strictly following a plan. Practices such as daily standups, sprints and retrospectives are the visible routines that carry those values. Continuous improvement is the habit of regularly inspecting how the team works, choosing a small change, trying it, and checking the result. A retrospective is a short, regular team meeting where the team looks back at the last period and agrees on one or two changes.

Why it works: practices without the mindset become rituals. People follow the steps but do not raise problems, because raising them feels unsafe or pointless. Improvement needs the team to believe that naming a problem leads to a fix. The leader's job is to make that belief true by acting on what the team says.

Worked example: Step 1, the retrospective notes that estimates are always too optimistic. Step 2, the leader does not just write the note down; she asks the team which single change would help most. Step 3, the team agrees to split stories into pieces no bigger than a day or two and to record how long each piece actually takes. Step 4, at the next retrospective they compare, and work finishes more predictably. Step 5, the change stays, and the team picks the next problem.

Common mistake: mandating practices as compliance, then counting attendance as success. The team holds standups but says nothing true in them, and the leader sees a green dashboard.

Consequence: retrospective action items pile up with no owner, and the same problems return sprint after sprint. This erodes the team's trust in the process itself, so the next honest retrospective is even less likely.

questions.prompt: A regional bank's card-dispute team of six holds a retrospective, which is a short, regular meeting where the team looks back at the last period and agrees on one or two changes. Step 1: the notes say disputes wait an average of four days before the fraud team picks them up. Step 2: the leader does not just log this. She asks the team which single change would help most. Step 3: the team agrees to stamp each dispute with the time it is handed to the fraud team, and to have one named person check the stamps each morning. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: the change stays, and the team chooses the next problem. Which statement fills step 4?
choices: The team waits until the quarterly business review to decide whether the stamps were worth keeping.
The leader reports the four-day wait to the bank's executive committee before the team tries anything else.
The team drops the stamps for two weeks so it can measure how much time they cost the staff.
At the next retrospective the team compares handoff waits with the previous period to see whether the change made a difference.
questions.why: Step 4 is the check that closes the try-and-check loop of continuous improvement: the team compares the result with the earlier period at its next retrospective, which is what the teaching describes as checking the result.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches a retrospective as the course defines it?
choices: A daily status report sent to the project manager, listing each task's percentage complete and who is blocked.
A planning session that fixes the full scope of the next three months before any work begins.
A long annual review in which each team member's performance is rated against a fixed plan set at the start of the year.
A short, regular team meeting where the team looks back at the last period and agrees on one or two changes.
questions.why: The course defines a retrospective as a short, regular team meeting that looks back at the last period and agrees on one or two changes, which matches only the second choice.

questions.prompt: A fintech team of eight holds a standup every weekday morning and attendance has been perfect for three months. Yet two blockers were reported only after each sprint ended, and team members say everything is fine at standup. Which response best fits the failure the course describes?
choices: The team needs stricter timekeeping rules so that every standup finishes within fifteen minutes, which will make people more focused.
The leader should replace the standups with a weekly written status report that each person completes alone at their own desk.
The practice has become a ritual without the mindset behind it, so the leader should act on what people say and make it safe to name problems.
Attendance is perfect, so the standup is clearly working, and the leader should add a second daily meeting to speed things up.
questions.why: The course's common mistake is mandating practices as compliance and counting attendance as success; the fix is to make raising problems feel safe and to act on what the team says, which only the last choice does.

questions.prompt: An insurance claims team agreed on five changes at its last retrospective. None of the five has a named owner, and the same delays appeared again in the following period. What is the most accurate reading and the right next move?
choices: Five changes attack more problems at once, so the team should keep the full list and review it again at the next quarterly planning session.
The retrospective should move to once a month so the list of changes can be cleared before each new period starts.
The team should limit each retrospective to one or two changes, and each change needs a named owner so it can be checked at the next meeting.
The leader should assign all five changes personally so that accountability for every item sits with one named person and the team does not have to argue about who does what.
questions.why: The course says a retrospective agrees on one or two changes and that action items with no owner pile up and let problems return, so limiting the count and naming owners is the correct response.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who thinks agile is just a set of meetings: what the agile mindset is, how continuous improvement depends on it, and one limit of relying on retrospectives alone to change a team.
lessons.modelAnswer: The agile mindset is the set of beliefs under the meetings: that working results and conversations with people matter more than plans and paperwork, and that change is normal. Continuous improvement is the habit of looking at how we work, trying one small change, and checking whether it helped. It depends on the mindset because people will only raise honest problems if they believe speaking up leads to a fix and is not punished. Retrospectives are the main place this happens, but they have a limit. A retrospective can agree on a change, yet if the team is afraid to disagree, or if the leader never acts on the action items, the change will not stick. So the retrospective needs a visible follow-through, and the leader has to protect people who raise problems. Without that, the meeting becomes a ritual.
rubricPoints: Defines the agile mindset as beliefs and priorities, distinct from the practices that express them
Explains continuous improvement as a repeated cycle of inspect, change a small thing, and check
Connects improvement to psychological safety: people must trust that raising problems leads to action
Names a concrete limit, such as unowned action items or a leader who does not follow through

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is explaining the mindset-versus-practice distinction in one's own words, which an explanation exercise tests more directly than any existing hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: A shared vision is a short, clear statement of what the product is for and what good looks like for the people it serves. Purpose is the reason behind the work: the outcome the organization actually cares about. A leader's job in agile is to keep the whole team pointed at that reason and to keep restating it, because the team makes many small choices every week that no plan can check in advance. Think of a ship's compass. The captain does not check it once at departure. Checking the heading and reminding the crew of the destination is part of the job, and it lets people make sound calls when conditions change.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has built a feature that works well and is on schedule, but the sales director says it does not help the company reach this quarter's goal of keeping existing customers. What would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Three terms matter here. A vision is the picture of the future the product is meant to help create. A purpose is the reason the work matters, usually framed as a business outcome. An organizational goal is a specific, measurable target the company is working toward this period, such as reducing customer churn by a set percentage. Product alignment means every item in the backlog can be traced to a goal or a stated purpose. Continuous communication means the why is repeated and discussed at planning, review, and day-to-day conversations, not presented once at kickoff.
Why it works: when people know the reason for the work, they can make trade-offs without asking permission for each one, and they can spot when a request does not serve the goal.
Worked example: the goal is to cut failed deliveries by 20 percent this half-year. Step 1: state the goal in one sentence where the team can see it. Step 2: for each backlog item, ask which goal measure it moves. Step 3: a dashboard redesign moves no measure of failed deliveries, so it is either reprioritized or justified as a separate decision. Step 4: at the sprint review, restate the goal and show the latest measure, then ask the team to explain in their own words how this sprint's work connects to it.
Common mistake: presenting the vision once in a kickoff deck and then assuming it is absorbed. People forget, new members never heard it, and the goal changes without anyone retelling the team.
Consequence: when the goal shifts mid-quarter and the team never heard, they keep building last quarter's priorities, and the product drifts away from what the organization needs.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy app team has a goal this quarter: cut refill lapses (patients who reach their refill date and do not reorder) from 22 percent to 15 percent. Step 1: the goal is written on the team board in one sentence. Step 2: the item 'add an auto-refill opt-in banner' is checked. It changes whether a patient reorders on time, so it moves the lapse measure and stays in the backlog. Step 3: the item 'change the app accent color to teal' is checked. No lapse measure moves, so it is parked or justified as a separate decision. Step 4 is missing. Mid-quarter the goal changes to 10 percent lapses by month end, and nobody tells the team. The next step that completes the alignment check is:
choices: Keep building the current sprint, since the team never formally approved the change.
Present the new goal once on a slide at the next all-hands and assume it will be absorbed.
Restate the new goal in one sentence where the team works, then recheck every backlog item still in play against the new measure.
Ask the team at the next planning to rank the items by how much they personally like them.
questions.why: When the goal changes, the team must hear the new target and every backlog item must be retraced against it, because the old alignment no longer holds.

questions.prompt: A team's backlog has 14 items. The product owner can state the product vision, but for 5 items nobody can name a goal measure or stated purpose they move. What does product alignment require the team to do with those 5?
choices: Leave them untouched until the next quarter's goals are published.
Keep them, since the sprint is already planned and the team has capacity.
Trace each one to a goal or stated purpose, and reprioritize or justify as a separate decision any that cannot be traced.
Give all five to the newest team member so that the work tests whether it matters.
questions.why: Product alignment means every backlog item can be traced to a goal or purpose, so untraceable items must be reprioritized or justified separately.

questions.prompt: A product team explained its purpose once at a kickoff workshop six months ago. The organization's goal moved last month, and two developers joined last week. Which outcome is the predictable consequence of this communication pattern?
choices: The team keeps the vision alive by default, since people usually remember a kickoff.
The team needs no change, because a stable vision does not need to be restated.
The team makes faster trade-offs, because the old purpose is still well remembered.
New members never heard the why, and the team may keep building last period's priorities while the product drifts from current needs.
questions.why: Continuous communication is needed because one-time presentations are forgotten, new members miss them, and goal changes go unnoticed.

questions.prompt: A sales lead asks the team to add a bulk export feature in the middle of a sprint. The team's goal is to reduce customer churn by 5 percent this half-year, and nothing in the export feature is linked to churn. What does a shared purpose let the team do here?
choices: Add the export immediately, since a request from a sales lead overrides the stated goal.
Ask the executive sponsor to rule on the request first, because only the sponsor can judge trade-offs.
Ignore the goal for this one request and reassess it at the next quarter's planning.
Decide on the spot whether the export serves the churn goal, and if it does not, defer it while sharing the reason with the lead.
questions.why: Knowing the reason for the work lets the team make the trade-off itself, without asking permission for each request, because the export does not move the churn measure.

lessons.explainPrompt: A new teammate asks why the team spends time at each sprint review restating the product goal when it is already written in the team charter. Explain to them what the restating does, and name one limit or cost of doing it too often.
lessons.modelAnswer: The charter is read once, but the goal has to survive hundreds of daily choices. Restating it at review and planning lets everyone check whether this sprint's work actually moved the outcome, and it gives people a shared reason to decline tempting extras. Repetition also surfaces drift: if someone cannot connect their current task to the goal, that signals the backlog or the goal has changed without the team being told. The limit is that the same words in every meeting turn into ritual, and people tune out. So the restatement should be brief, paired with new evidence such as the latest measure or customer feedback, and should ask the team to explain the goal in their own words rather than have the leader recite it. Ceremony that takes more time than the team spends acting on the goal has stopped doing its job.
rubricPoints: Restating the goal lets the team check whether current work actually moves the outcome.
Repetition helps people make trade-offs and decline work that does not serve the purpose.
Repeated restating can surface drift when goals or backlog priorities change unnoticed.
Overdoing it becomes empty ritual, so restatements should be brief and backed by new evidence.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the link between the goal and daily work back to a teammate, including its limits, is the core skill here and no listed mission or engine covers it.

lessons.plain: When two people on a team clash, the visible argument is rarely the real problem. This objective is about pausing long enough to ask where the disagreement comes from and how far it reaches. A fight about a deadline might really be about unclear priorities, a clash of working styles, or a rule the whole group never agreed on. As the person facilitating, your job is to help the people involved examine the problem together and find an answer that meets their underlying needs, instead of picking a winner or ignoring the tension.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two team members argue at every stand-up about who should review pull requests. Before deciding who is right, what would you want to find out first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A conflict is a disagreement that is visible and affects how work gets done. Its root cause is the underlying reason it keeps coming back, which is often different from the trigger that starts each argument. The conflict level describes how wide the disagreement reaches: inside one person (an unclear personal priority), between two people, within a team, between teams, or between the team and the wider organization, such as a shared policy or funding rule. Naming the level tells you who must be in the room. A collaborative approach focuses on each party's interests, meaning the reasons they want something, rather than their positions, meaning the specific outcome they demand. When interests overlap, the group can often design an option that serves everyone.

Why it works: people defend positions hard, but they let go of them once they see their real need can be met another way. Asking why, then comparing reasons, moves the group from winning an argument to solving a problem.

Worked example: two developers argue every stand-up over whether a feature branch should merge before a dependency is reviewed. Step 1: the trigger is the stand-up argument. Step 2: ask each person why. One wants to avoid blocking the release; the other wants to avoid a broken main branch. Step 3: both interests are valid and shared, so the root cause is that the team has no agreed merge rule. Step 4: the level is intra-team, not personal, so the fix belongs to the whole team. Step 5: the group agrees on a rule and tests it for two sprints.

Common mistake: declaring a winner, or treating every conflict as a personality problem. If the real cause is a team-wide gap and you only coach the two developers, the argument returns next sprint.

Consequence: in a running delivery pipeline, a misdiagnosed merge fight can mean either a release slips or unreviewed code reaches production. Diagnose the cause and level before choosing an approach.

questions.prompt: A design lead and an engineering lead at a logistics firm argue at every sprint planning about whether a screen mockup must be approved before a story can enter the sprint. Worked so far: Step 1, the trigger is the planning-meeting argument. Step 2, asking why: the design lead wants to avoid engineers building the wrong screen, and the engineering lead wants to avoid sprints where stories sit idle waiting on design. Step 3 is missing. Step 4, the conflict spans two departments, so it is between teams, not personal, and both leads must be involved in fixing it.
choices: Coach the design lead to be more flexible, since the problem is mainly one person's attitude.
Postpone the argument to the next quarterly review and let the sprints run as they are.
Name the root cause as the absence of an agreed approval rule between design and engineering, which both interests point to.
Declare the engineering lead the winner because engineering owns the sprint capacity.
questions.why: Both leads' interests are valid and shared, so the root cause is the missing agreed rule between the two groups, which is the step that lets the fix be designed for everyone.

questions.prompt: A product sponsor and a delivery team keep clashing over a company-wide rule from finance that requires all projects to be funded by a fixed annual budget cycle. Which conflict level does this disagreement sit at?
choices: Between two people, because the sponsor and one team member are arguing.
Within one team, because the whole team feels the pressure equally.
Between the team and the wider organization, because the rule itself is set outside the team.
Inside one person, because the sponsor has an unclear personal priority.
questions.why: A shared funding rule set by the wider organization places the disagreement between the team and the organization, so the people who own that rule must be part of the resolution.

questions.prompt: A coach sees a stakeholder insist that a feature ships on a fixed Friday date, and the team's reply is only to push back on the date. Which statement correctly separates the stakeholder's interest from the stakeholder's position?
choices: The position is the team wanting more time, and the interest is the stakeholder's authority.
Both the date and the hotfix are positions, because neither describes a reason for the stakeholder's choice.
The position is avoiding rushed hotfixes, and the interest is the fixed Friday date.
The position is the specific Friday date being demanded, and the interest is the reason behind wanting it, such as avoiding a rushed hotfix later.
questions.why: A position is the specific outcome a party demands, while the interest is the underlying reason they want it, and the stakeholder's reason here is avoiding rushed fixes after release.

questions.prompt: Two team members clash at every retrospective over whose story estimates should count. The coach concludes both are difficult people and coaches each one privately, but the argument returns the next sprint. What is the most likely mistake in this approach?
choices: Coaching the two members privately, since private coaching is never useful in a team conflict.
Declaring one estimate as correct instead of hearing both sides first.
Treating a team-wide gap, such as no agreed estimating rule, as a personality problem to be solved by coaching only the two people involved.
Choosing to hold the retrospective more often, which adds meetings without addressing the cause.
questions.why: If the real cause is a team-wide gap and only the two individuals are coached, the underlying reason stays in place and the argument comes back, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns about.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says two engineers just do not get along and suggests moving one of them to another team. Explain to your teammate how you would identify the root cause and level of this conflict, and what collaborative approach you would try first, including one limit of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not accept the personality explanation yet. First I would find the level: is this really between two people, or is it a team-wide gap that shows up between them? Then I would meet each person separately and ask why they hold their position, so I hear their interests rather than just their demands. If both want the same outcome, such as a stable release, the real cause is usually a missing shared rule, like an agreed merge or review standard. I would bring both people and the team together to design that rule and test it for a sprint or two. The limit is that interest-based discussion only works if both people are willing to share their reasons honestly and the team has the authority to change the rule. If one party's need conflicts with an organizational constraint, the conflict has moved to a higher level and needs that decision-maker involved.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes the trigger of the conflict from its underlying root cause
Identifies the conflict level (individual, interpersonal, intra-team, inter-team, or organizational) to decide who must be involved
Uses interests rather than positions to find shared needs
Proposes a collaborative fix, such as an agreed team rule, instead of picking a winner
Names a real limit, such as a constraint that sits above the team's authority

suggested.rationale: Conflict diagnosis and collaborative facilitation are best proven by explaining the reasoning aloud, since no listed mission or planned engine simulates team dynamics.

lessons.plain: A product backlog is the single ordered list of everything that might be built for a product. Refining it means keeping that list healthy: making vague items clear, splitting big ones into smaller pieces, putting the most valuable items at the top, and estimating effort as a whole team. Think of a shared shopping list that gets tidied every week: entries are written clearly, huge entries are broken into separate purchases, and the things you need most move to the front. Refinement is ongoing rather than a single meeting, and it involves customers and stakeholders who can say what matters and why.
lessons.guessPrompt: A backlog contains an item called 'Improve checkout' that the team estimates at 40 days of work. Before any teaching, what do you think should happen to that item before the team commits to it, and who should be involved?
lessons.teach: A backlog item is one entry in the product backlog, the ordered list of work the product might need. Refining the backlog means getting items ready for planning: clarifying what they mean, decomposing them (splitting a large item into smaller items, such as breaking an epic, which is a big theme, into user stories, which are small pieces of user-visible value), prioritizing them (ordering by value, risk and dependencies), and sizing them (estimating relative effort). Sizing is done collectively: the team estimates together, often with planning poker, where members reveal numbers at the same time so that one person's opinion does not anchor the others. Disagreement is useful, because it exposes different assumptions. Refinement works because small, clear items can be finished and checked with customers sooner, and ordering by value means the team spends effort on what pays off first. Worked example: 'Improve checkout' is 40 days. Step 1: the product owner and a customer representative state the goal, which is reducing abandoned carts. Step 2: the item is split into guest checkout, saved card payment, address autocomplete and confirmation email. Step 3: stakeholders rank guest checkout highest, because most abandonment happens at the login step. Step 4: the team sizes guest checkout together; one engineer flags a payment-provider dependency, so the item is split again. Common mistake: letting one person size or prioritize alone, or refining once and never revisiting. The consequence is that oversized items hide risk, the team commits to a 40-day item, and nothing reaches customers for weeks.

questions.prompt: A regional bank's product owner, Ana, has a 60-day backlog item called 'Modernize mortgage pre-approval'. Many applicants quit the pre-approval form partway through. Step 1: Ana and a branch manager state the goal as reducing applicants who abandon the form. Step 2: the item is split into four smaller items: document upload, rate display, identity check, and status tracker. Step 3: stakeholders rank document upload highest, because most applicants quit at the document step. Step 4: the team sizes document upload together using planning poker, where everyone reveals a hidden estimate at the same moment. The estimates come back as 3 and 13. What should the team do next?
choices: The two people who estimated 3 and 13 explain their assumptions, the team discusses the difference, and then they re-estimate.
Ana picks the 3, since the lower estimate is probably the more confident one, and the item is committed.
The item is removed from the backlog because a wide spread means the item cannot be sized at all.
The team averages the two numbers to 8, writes it down, and moves on without talking about it.
questions.why: Disagreement exposes different assumptions, so the team should discuss the gap and re-estimate, not hide it through averaging or let one person decide.

questions.prompt: In backlog refinement, what does it mean to size work collectively using planning poker, and why is the reveal done at the same time?
choices: Members reveal their estimates simultaneously so that no one's opinion anchors, or pulls, the others before they have formed their own.
Stakeholders estimate the work in money, and the team converts the figure into story points afterward.
Each member privately writes a fixed size, the product owner collects them, and the final size is the one she chooses.
The team estimates in turn, with the most senior engineer speaking first so others can follow her lead.
questions.why: Simultaneous reveal stops one person's number from anchoring the rest, which is the reason the teaching text gives for the method.

questions.prompt: A product owner at a furniture retailer sizes and ranks all 25 backlog items alone during a Friday afternoon, then the list is never revisited while the team works through the next two months. What is the most likely consequence for the running product?
choices: Oversized items hide risk, the team commits to large items it has not sized together, and little reaches customers for weeks.
Ranking by one person makes the backlog order more consistent, so customers see features sooner than before.
Nothing changes, because sizing only affects the team's internal reporting and not the product.
The team gets too many chances to discuss assumptions, which slows delivery by a few days.
questions.why: The teaching text names one-person sizing and never revisiting as the common mistake, with oversized items hiding risk and delaying customer-visible delivery as the consequence.

questions.prompt: A retailer has an epic called 'Customer self-service returns'. Which of these is the best example of a user story that could come from splitting it?
choices: Create a returns database table with indexed columns for speed.
Write the full returns project plan with milestones for the year.
Hire two more engineers to start the returns work next quarter.
A customer can start a return for one item from their order history and see a return label.
questions.why: A user story is a small piece of user-visible value, and only the option describing a customer doing one thing from their order history fits that description.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says refinement is just tidying the backlog, and that the product owner can do it alone over the weekend. Explain to them what refinement involves, why the team sizes items together, and one limit or tradeoff of splitting items too finely.
lessons.modelAnswer: Refinement is the ongoing work of making backlog items clear, splitting large ones, ordering them by value, and estimating them, and it should involve customers and stakeholders for clarity and priority. The product owner can set priorities, but the team needs to see the items to know what they actually mean and how big they are. Sizing together matters because each person knows different risks; when estimates differ widely, that gap usually reveals a hidden assumption worth discussing before work begins. The tradeoff of splitting too finely is that items become so small they lose user-visible value, and the team spends time tracking many tiny pieces instead of delivering a working outcome. Each split item should still be something a customer could notice or check. Refinement is a continuing habit, so new information should trigger another pass.
rubricPoints: Refinement covers clarifying, decomposing, prioritizing and sizing backlog items, not just tidying the list.
Customers and stakeholders should help clarify and rank items, with the team involved in sizing.
Collaborative sizing exposes different assumptions and reduces single-person bias.
Splitting too finely can strip out user-visible value and create tracking overhead.
Refinement is continuous and should be repeated as new information arrives.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises backlog refinement, and explaining the technique back to a teammate is the core skill for this objective.

lessons.plain: An increment is a slice of finished, usable work that a team delivers in one cycle. Managing increments means making sure each slice is chosen because it matters to the business, that the team agrees on one short sentence describing what the slice is meant to achieve, and that real users or stakeholders see it early so the team learns whether it was the right thing to build. Think of a cook who makes a small tasting batch before serving the whole dinner. The point is not only to cook, but to check the flavour while there is still time to change it. This lesson covers three habits: linking increments to priorities, writing increment goals, and using early feedback as evidence of value.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has two weeks and a long backlog. Their manager says, 'Just finish as many items as you can.' What is one thing that would be missing from that plan, and why could the business still lose out even if every item is finished?
lessons.teach:
An increment is the slice of working product a team completes in one cycle, and it should be something that could be used or released. A business priority is the outcome the organization ranks highest right now, such as cutting the time dispatchers spend finding vehicles. An increment goal is one short sentence stating the outcome the slice should achieve, and it is different from a task list. Early feedback is evidence gathered from real users or stakeholders before the slice is final, such as a demonstration, a pilot or a usage measure.

Why it works: a list of finished tasks shows activity, not value. A goal lets the team judge trade-offs, so when time runs short they drop the least useful task rather than the outcome that matters most. Feedback then tests whether the goal was the right one while changes are still cheap.

Worked example, a fleet dispatch tool. Step 1: the priority is faster vehicle lookup. Step 2: pick backlog items that serve it, such as a live map of positions and search by vehicle ID. Step 3: write the increment goal: dispatchers can locate any active vehicle in under 10 seconds. Step 4: at the review, two dispatchers time the search, taking 25 seconds on the old tool and 12 on the new build. Step 5: they ask for a depot filter, which goes into the next increment's backlog rather than expanding this one.

Common mistake: treating the increment as a bag of tasks. When one task slips, the team ships anyway and nobody checks the goal, so the work looks complete while dispatchers still wait.

Consequence: in a running system, this gap shows up as features that go live, dashboards that stay green, and no change in the measure the business actually cares about.

questions.prompt: A hospital ward team's current business priority is shorter waits for discharge paperwork. For this increment they select two backlog items: an electronic discharge checklist and a flag showing when a patient's medicines are ready. Step 1 (priority) and Step 2 (backlog items) are done. Step 3, writing the increment goal, is still blank. Step 4 will be a pilot on a live shift, and Step 5 will route any new requests into the next increment's backlog. Which sentence correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Finish the checklist screen and the medicine-ready flag before the sprint ends.
Ward nurses can finish discharge paperwork for any ready patient in under 15 minutes.
Improve discharge handling across all wards during the next quarter.
Show the checklist to the hospital board at the end-of-cycle review.
questions.why: A correct increment goal is one short sentence stating a measurable outcome tied to the priority, which the first option (a task list), the third (too vague to judge), and the fourth (a feedback event, not an outcome) all fail to be.

questions.prompt: A product owner writes the following as the increment goal for a payroll tool: 'Build the timesheet import, the overtime calculator, and the approval email.' Which statement best explains why this is not a valid increment goal?
choices: It should contain the name of the payroll system vendor to be useful.
It is valid, because approval emails are always the outcome users care about.
It lists tasks, so when one slips the team has no outcome to judge which trade-off matters most.
It names too few features to justify a full cycle of work.
questions.why: An increment goal states the outcome the slice should achieve; a list of tasks shows activity, and without an outcome the team cannot decide which work to drop when time runs short.

questions.prompt: A library's current business priority is getting returned books back on shelves faster. Partway through an increment, a branch manager asks for a new report of overdue fines. What is the most appropriate response under the increment-management approach?
choices: Place the request in the next increment's backlog and keep this increment's goal unchanged.
Stop the increment and restart planning around fines, since the new request is more urgent.
Add the report to the current increment, since the team is already working on the library tool.
Expand the current increment's goal so the report is covered by the same outcome.
questions.why: Requests that do not serve the current increment goal go into the next increment's backlog rather than widening the current slice, which keeps the goal stable and the scope judged against the outcome.

questions.prompt: A team demonstrates a new customer-onboarding flow to three pilot users at the end of its increment. Two of them finish the flow more slowly than on the old form, and the team's goal was 'new customers complete onboarding in under five minutes.' What does this early feedback most directly tell the team?
choices: The team should finish all remaining tasks before reading the feedback, so the demo is not disrupted.
The feedback is unreliable because only three users were involved, so the goal can be ignored.
The goal itself may be the wrong target or the build may not yet serve it, and the team should revisit both while changes are still cheap.
The team should assume the old form was better and abandon the increment entirely.
questions.why: Early feedback tests whether the increment goal was the right one while changes are still cheap, so a slower result signals a need to revisit the goal or the build rather than ignoring it or shipping anyway.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to agile why the team should write one increment goal and gather early feedback before the increment is finished. Name one limit or tradeoff of doing this.
lessons.modelAnswer: The increment goal is a single sentence saying what outcome this slice should achieve, such as dispatchers finding any vehicle in under 10 seconds. Without it, the team can finish a pile of tasks and still have no proof the business gained anything. When a task runs late, the goal tells us which work to cut, because we protect the outcome rather than every item. Early feedback, like letting dispatchers time the new search during the review, tests whether the goal was right while changes are cheap. The tradeoff is that feedback arrives on partial work, so people may judge an unfinished screen harshly or ask for changes that belong in a later increment. The team has to keep those requests in the backlog and not reopen the current slice.
rubricPoints: An increment goal states the outcome to achieve, not a list of tasks.
Early feedback from real users or stakeholders tests whether the goal was the right one.
When time is short, the goal guides which work to drop.
A real limit: feedback on partial work can be premature, so new requests go to the backlog.

suggested.rationale: A scenario where the learner must choose which backlog items serve a priority and set a goal adds more than reading alone, and no listed mission covers this directly.

lessons.plain: Work visualization means showing the team's work in a shared picture that everyone can see and update, such as a board with columns for to do, doing and done, or a simple list with each item's current stage. The point is that anyone can see where work is stuck, how much is in progress, and what is finished without having to ask someone. Choosing a technique means picking a picture that fits the team's situation. Educating the team means making sure everyone knows what each column and rule means. Keeping the data current means the picture matches reality, because an out-of-date board can mislead people more than having no board at all.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team's board shows six cards in the 'In progress' column, but three of those cards have not been touched in over a week and two people on them are on leave. What is the most likely problem with the board, and what would you change first?
lessons.teach: A work item is one unit of work the team tracks, such as a feature, a bug fix, or a task. A visualization is a shared display of those items. A board is the most common form: each column is a stage (for example Ready, Building, Testing, Done), and each item is a card that moves left to right as it progresses. Work-in-progress, or WIP, is the number of items currently started but not finished. A WIP limit is a cap set on how many items a column may hold at once. Status data is the information on the board: where each item sits and when it last moved. Why this works: people carry status in their heads, and that memory is incomplete and out of date. A shared picture lets the team see bottlenecks and idle stages at a glance. Worked example: the Building column has a WIP limit of 3. On Monday three stories are in Building and a fourth is ready. It waits in Ready. On Tuesday the Testing column is empty while Building is full. The team sees the imbalance and two people help finish the Building items so they can move into Testing. Common mistake: the board is updated in a weekly batch, so cards reflect last week rather than today. Consequence: the team plans around work that already finished or is blocked, and managers make decisions from wrong data. A board that is kept current is a working tool; a board that is not is a source of false confidence.

questions.prompt: A payments support team uses a board with the columns Ready, Developing, Review and Done. The Developing column has a WIP limit of 2. On Monday both Developing slots are full and a third ticket waits in Ready. On Tuesday evening one Developing ticket is finished, but its card still shows Developing because nobody moved it. On Wednesday morning the lead plans the day around that ticket as if it were still in progress. The step that was missed is that the finished card should have been moved to Done on Tuesday evening, so the board showed the true state of work. Which action would have kept the board current?
choices: Move the finished card to Done as soon as the work is complete, so the board shows today's state.
Move the finished card to Review and wait for the weekly report to confirm it.
Delete the finished card so the Developing count drops and a new ticket can start.
Leave the finished card in Developing until the Friday batch update.
questions.why: Keeping status data current means moving each card when its state changes, so the board reflects the actual position of the work rather than a stale memory of it.

questions.prompt: In a team's board, what does the status data consist of?
choices: The team's weekly meeting agenda and its attendance list.
The record of where each item sits on the board and when it last moved.
The list of customer complaints gathered over the last quarter.
The total number of hours each person logged during the month.
questions.why: Status data is defined as the information on the board, namely each item's position and the time it last moved.

questions.prompt: A logistics team updates its board only at the end of each week. On Tuesday, a manager reads a card still marked Blocked, though the blocker was cleared on Monday. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The board becomes more accurate because the old information is preserved for review.
The manager may escalate an item that is already unblocked and spend effort on the wrong problem.
Finished cards move themselves into Done so the manager sees them sooner.
The team automatically hits its WIP limit because blocked cards count against it.
questions.why: A board that is not kept current gives false confidence, so decisions made from its stale status can target work that has already changed.

questions.prompt: A design team of six people has a WIP limit of 3 on its Sketching column. Sketching is full, the Review column is empty, and two sketches are nearly finished. Which response best uses the board to fix the imbalance?
choices: Start a fourth sketch so that nobody on the team sits idle.
Help finish the sketches that are in progress so they can move into Review.
Add a new column called Maybe for cards whose status is uncertain.
Raise the Sketching limit to six so that no card ever has to wait.
questions.why: The board shows a full upstream stage and an empty downstream stage, so the right move is to clear work out of the full stage by helping finish it rather than adding or hiding work.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who thinks a visible board is just decoration how choosing a work-visualization technique and keeping its status data current affects the team's decisions. Name one limit or tradeoff of the technique you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: A board is only useful if it changes what people do. I would explain that we pick the visualization to fit the question we need answered: a board with WIP limits shows where work piles up, while a simple list may be enough for a small team with few stages. Every technique has a limit. A board shows flow well but says little about how much total scope remains, so for that we would also need a burn-up chart or similar. The data has to be current, because a stale card sends people to plan around work that is already done or blocked. So I would ask the team to move cards as they go and review the board daily, not update it in a weekly batch. When the board is accurate, the team can act on it: stop starting new work when a column is full, and swarm on what is stuck.
rubricPoints: Explains that the visualization should be chosen to answer a specific question about flow or progress.
States that status data must be kept current, or the board misleads decisions.
Names a real limit or tradeoff of the chosen technique, such as not showing total remaining scope.
Connects the shared picture to a concrete team action, such as respecting WIP limits or swarming a bottleneck.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a technique and judging whether shared status data is trustworthy is best practiced by reasoning through a realistic board scenario, which no listed mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: Value delivery means being clear, before and after building something, about what 'worth it' actually means. A team can ship many features and still fail its users if nobody agreed on what success looks like. This objective is about writing down measurable success criteria for a product change, then checking whether those results really happened. It also means remembering that value has conditions: the change must stay sustainable for the people who maintain it, keep data safe, and follow the rules that apply to the business. Think of a recipe. Finishing the dish is not enough if it is inedible or breaks the kitchen's safety codes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team ships a new feature on the planned date and everyone is happy. Name two things you would want to know before deciding the release was actually a success.
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A success criterion is a measurable statement of what must be true for a change to count as valuable, such as a target number or a condition that can be checked. An outcome is the real-world change you want, such as more customers finishing checkout. An output is what you built, such as a new button. Teams are tempted to report outputs, but value lives in outcomes. Sustainability means the team can keep delivering and maintaining the change at a steady pace without burnout or hidden debt. Security means the change does not weaken protection of systems or data. Compliance means it meets the rules, contracts or regulations that bind the business. Guard conditions are the security, compliance and sustainability limits that must hold while you chase the main target.

Why it works. Agreeing on measurable criteria before work starts gives the backlog a test. Each item is judged against the result it is meant to move, so low-value work can be dropped. The check afterwards closes the loop. A lagging indicator measures the result after release, such as weekly completed orders. A leading indicator gives an early signal, such as the error rate in the first hour.

Worked example. A product owner wants faster checkout. Step 1: write the target as checkout completing in under 2 seconds at the 95th percentile, with the payment failure rate staying below 0.5 percent. Step 2: add guard conditions: no card numbers written to logs (security), the change passes the required payment review (compliance), and no weekend fix is needed to keep it running (sustainability). Step 3: after release, measure all of these for two weeks. If latency falls to 1.4 seconds but failures rise to 0.9 percent, the release did not achieve the targeted result, even though it shipped on time.

Common mistake. Declaring success because the feature was delivered. Output is not outcome. A second mistake is tracking one headline metric while ignoring the guard conditions, so the number improves while the system becomes less secure or harder to run.

Consequence. In a running system, a checkout that is faster but leaks card data, or fails under load, will be rolled back or trigger a compliance incident, so the apparent win becomes a cost. Value is confirmed only when the measured results meet the criteria and the guard conditions still hold.

questions.prompt: A regional parcel company's tracking team wants fewer 'where is my parcel?' phone calls. Step 1: the target is written as calls per 1,000 deliveries falling from 40 to under 25 within four weeks, with the tracking page loading in under 3 seconds for 95 percent of visits. Step 2: the guard conditions are that the tracking page shows no recipient home address (security), the page keeps only 30 days of delivery data as the national postal rule requires (compliance), and the support on-call rota is not paged more than twice a week (sustainability). Step 3 is missing. The team has released the page and wants to know whether it worked. Which action completes Step 3?
choices: Count the number of tracking-page features released and report that total to the steering group.
Add a new headline metric for page views and wait until the number rises before reviewing the calls.
Ask the customer service manager whether the new page feels helpful, and treat a positive answer as proof of value.
Measure calls per 1,000 deliveries, page load time, and all three guard conditions over a fixed window after release, then compare each result with its criterion.
questions.why: Confirming value means measuring the targeted result and the guard conditions after release and comparing them with the agreed criteria, not reporting shipped work or opinion.

questions.prompt: A team reports to its sponsor that it has 'delivered a new reporting dashboard with 12 charts'. Which statement best describes what the team has reported?
choices: A guard condition, because the dashboard is a security feature for managers.
An outcome, because the charts are visible to users every day.
An output, because it describes what was built rather than the real-world change it was meant to cause.
A success criterion, because it names a measurable number of charts.
questions.why: Twelve charts is something built, which is an output; the outcome would be the change in decisions or behaviour the dashboard was meant to produce.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team's picking app cuts average pick time from 90 seconds to 60 seconds. However, the change needed a weekly manual fix by the one engineer who understands it, and the team now pages that engineer every night. Based on the idea of guard conditions, what is the correct conclusion?
choices: The release is valuable only if the engineer agrees to keep working nights.
The release did not confirm value, because the sustainability guard condition is failing even though the headline metric improved.
The release achieved its targeted result, because pick time fell by a third.
The team should drop the pick-time target entirely because it caused the paging.
questions.why: Tracking one headline metric while a guard condition such as sustainability breaks means the apparent win is not confirmed as value.

questions.prompt: A booking app team releases a change and tracks two numbers: the error rate in the first hour after release, and total monthly bookings measured at month end. Which description correctly classifies these two indicators?
choices: Both are leading indicators because both are measured on the live system.
The first-hour error rate is a lagging indicator and the monthly bookings are a leading indicator.
The first-hour error rate is a leading indicator giving an early signal, and the monthly bookings are a lagging indicator measuring the result after release.
Both are lagging indicators because both are measured after the release.
questions.why: A leading indicator gives an early signal soon after release, while a lagging indicator measures the result over a longer period after release, so the first-hour error rate leads and monthly bookings lag.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a shipped change actually delivered value, and name one limit or tradeoff of the measure you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing down the target before we build: a measurable result, like checkout finishing in under two seconds for most users, plus guard conditions such as no new security exposure and no extra manual work for the team. After release I would measure both the target and the guards over an agreed period, compared against a baseline we recorded beforehand. The main limit is that a metric can improve for the wrong reasons. Faster checkout might come from skipping a validation step, so the guard conditions matter as much as the headline number. Another tradeoff is timing: lagging measures like weekly orders confirm the result but arrive late, while leading signals like error rate arrive early but may not perfectly predict the business outcome. So I would report both, and say plainly when the evidence is still too thin to call it a win.
rubricPoints: Defines a measurable success criterion before the work starts, not after release.
Separates outputs (what was built) from outcomes (the result achieved).
Includes guard conditions for security, compliance and sustainability alongside the main target.
Names a real limit or tradeoff of the chosen measure, such as gaming a metric or lagging versus leading timing.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the success criteria and guard conditions back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Seeking early feedback means showing people who care about the result a small, working piece of it early and often, instead of waiting until everything is finished. Imagine baking a cake and tasting it only after the frosting is set. If it needs more sugar, you are stuck. Taste the batter along the way and the fix is cheap. In delivery work, the small pieces are called increments, and the people whose opinion shapes the result are stakeholders. Getting their reactions on a regular rhythm lets the team learn what is wrong while changing it is still inexpensive.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has four months to build a new feature for a dispatch office. Option A: the team builds quietly and shows the office once, at the end. Option B: the team shows a small working part every two weeks. Which option is more likely to end with the office getting what it actually needed, and why?
lessons.teach:
An increment is a small, usable slice of the finished product that works end to end, even if it covers only a few cases. Stakeholders are anyone affected by the result: the people who use it, the people who fund it, and the people who run it. Seeking early feedback means putting increments in front of stakeholders on a fixed cadence, meaning a regular interval such as every two weeks, and acting on what they say.

Why it works: requirements are guesses until someone uses the thing. People often cannot describe what they want in the abstract but recognise it at once when they see it. Feedback gathered while a change is still a few hours of work costs far less than feedback gathered after a month of building on a wrong assumption. Each cycle shrinks the gap between what was built and what is needed.

Worked example: a team builds a vehicle-status view for dispatchers over twelve weeks. In week 2 the team shows a working list of vehicles with a basic status column. A dispatcher says the list should sort by how long each vehicle has been idle. The team changes the sort order in an afternoon. In week 4 a second increment adds a map pin, and the dispatcher asks for a colour for overdue vehicles. Another small change. Compare a team that waits until week 12 to show anything: the same requests arrive then, along with dozens of other unexamined assumptions that are now expensive to unwind.

Common mistake: calling a slide deck or a status report feedback. Feedback needs a working increment and a response that changes something. Another mistake is collecting input only from the sponsor who funds the work, not from the people who will use it every day.

Consequence: in a running system, a late discovery means the wrong thing goes live, staff build workarounds around it, and those workarounds become the next problem to fix. Early feedback turns a long, risky bet into a series of small, checkable steps.

questions.prompt: A small accounts team at a regional courier firm builds an invoice-approval screen. Stakeholders here means anyone affected by the result, and a cadence means a fixed interval between feedback checkpoints. The steps so far: Step 1 (week 1): the team shows a working screen with one approval path to the finance lead, who funds the work. Step 2 (same week): the lead says approvals should go to the budget owner first, and the team changes the routing that afternoon. Step 3 is missing from this trace. Step 4 (week 3): the two clerks who process invoices every day report a missing 'query' button, and the team adds it before the next checkpoint. Which completes Step 3 correctly?
choices: The team emails the finance lead a status report summarising the routing change for sign-off.
The team waits until week 3 to show the full approval module, including the routing and query features together.
The team shows the revised screen to the two clerks who use it every day and asks what they would change.
The team asks the clerks to sign off a written requirements document describing the screen before any more building.
questions.why: Step 3 is the early feedback from people who use the screen every day, shown as a working increment and acted on, which is the pattern the earlier steps establish.

questions.prompt: A team finishes two weeks of work that adds a database table and an internal service, but no screen a user can touch yet. Using the definition of an increment (a small, usable slice of the finished product that works end to end), what is the best judgment?
choices: It is an increment only if the sponsor approves the database design in a status report.
It is an increment, because the table can be demonstrated to the funder.
It is an increment, because every finished piece of code counts toward one.
Not yet an increment: it must work end to end for someone affected by it.
questions.why: An increment must be usable end to end by someone affected by the result, so internal plumbing alone does not qualify.

questions.prompt: A team collects feedback only through a monthly status report sent to the sponsor who funds the work, and shows the product for the first time at project close. What is the main risk of this approach?
choices: The team should add more features before showing anything so the first demo is worth the time.
Requirements are untested guesses, and the people who use the result react to it only after changing it has become expensive.
The sponsor's view is always the most accurate, so the risk is low.
The monthly report is acceptable because it is a regular cadence.
questions.why: Requirements are guesses until someone uses the thing, and feedback from the sponsor alone, delivered only at the end, delays the discovery of wrong assumptions.

questions.prompt: A team shows a working increment to stakeholders every six months. Which judgment best matches the idea of seeking early feedback on a regular cadence?
choices: Frequency does not matter as long as the final delivery is polished.
Six months is ideal because stakeholders need time to form considered opinions.
Six months is too infrequent; a fixed interval such as every two weeks keeps each change small and cheap.
Feedback should only be gathered once every requirement has been finished.
questions.why: The idea is that regular, short intervals keep each correction small, so six-monthly checkpoints leave too much unexamined work between feedback points.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who thinks demos are a waste of time why we seek feedback on small increments every sprint rather than only at the end of the project. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Showing a small working increment every sprint means we learn what stakeholders actually want while changes are still cheap. If we wait until the end, we only discover wrong assumptions when rework is expensive and the schedule is nearly gone. Each review gives a fixed moment when the people who use the product can react, and we act on their input before building further. The tradeoff is that frequent feedback can pull the team toward whatever was requested most recently, so the product can drift without a clear goal. Stakeholders also have limited time, so reviews can become tiring or get skipped. We manage this by keeping the product goal visible, weighing each piece of feedback against it, and keeping each increment small enough to review in a short session.
rubricPoints: Increments are small, working slices shown on a regular cadence, not one delivery at the end.
Feedback comes from the stakeholders who use or depend on the result, not only the sponsor.
Early feedback is cheap to act on because changes are small while assumptions are still open.
A real limit: frequent feedback can cause drift, so each piece must be weighed against the product goal.

suggested.rationale: That mission covers Scrum for an operations engineer, where the sprint review is the regular feedback point this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: Agile metrics are a small set of numbers that show how work is actually moving: how long items take, how many are stuck, and whether the team finishes what it starts. Picking the right ones matters because a number that helps a team coach itself can mislead an executive, and the reverse is also true. Radiating a metric means putting it where people see it without having to ask, such as a wall or a shared page that updates. The purpose is not to grade people but to notice trouble early and decide what to change next. Think of a car dashboard: the driver needs speed and fuel, while the mechanic needs engine temperature and fault codes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team's sprint velocity has risen for three sprints, yet customers still complain that features arrive late. Which single measure would you add to find out why, and who would you show it to first?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a number tracked over time. Agile teams use flow metrics. Cycle time is the elapsed days from when a piece of work starts until it is done. Lead time is the elapsed days from when a request is made until it is delivered. Throughput is how many items finish in a period. Work in progress, or WIP, is the count of items started but not yet finished. Velocity, the points a team completes per sprint, is a planning tool meant for that one team. Each metric answers a different question for a different audience. The team asks what is blocking it today, the product owner asks when a feature will land, and leaders ask whether value reaches customers quickly.

Why it works: these measures are linked. Little's Law, stated simply, says that in a steady system the average WIP equals throughput multiplied by average cycle time. If throughput stays flat while WIP climbs, cycle time must climb too. A team can read that relationship on one chart and spot a slowdown before customers complain.

Worked example: a team of six finishes 5 items a week on average, and its board holds 15 items in progress. Step 1: divide WIP by throughput, 15 divided by 5, which gives 3 weeks. Step 2: the average item therefore takes about 3 weeks, far beyond the 1 week the team expects. Step 3: the decision is to stop pulling new work until WIP falls to about 5 or 6, then recheck cycle time next sprint.

Common mistake: turning velocity into a target. When people are rewarded for higher points, estimates inflate and the number stops meaning anything. Use metrics to ask questions, not to grade people.

Consequence: when cycle time rises on a live product, fixes and features queue behind each other, so incidents and customer requests wait longer. Flow metrics belong on a visible board or shared dashboard, reviewed at a regular cadence, and each one should suggest an action a team member could take the same day.

questions.prompt: A design studio finishes 12 client requests a month on average, and its board holds 30 requests in progress. Little's Law says that in a steady system average cycle time equals average WIP divided by throughput, so the studio's average cycle time is 30 divided by 12, which is 2.5 months. The studio wants cycle time back to 1 month. Step 3, which is missing from this trace, asks: at the same throughput of 12 requests a month, what average WIP level brings cycle time down to 1 month, and what should the studio cap its board at?
choices: Cap WIP at 6, because half the current throughput gives the target
Cap WIP at 30, because the current level is already the right size
Cap WIP at 2.5, because that is the current cycle time in months
Cap WIP at 12, because 1 month times 12 requests a month gives 12 items
questions.why: Rearranging Little's Law gives WIP equal to throughput times cycle time, so 12 requests a month times a 1-month target gives a WIP cap of 12.

questions.prompt: A product owner at a logistics firm asks when the next set of shipping-label features will reach customers. Which metric answers that audience's question most directly?
choices: The number of open defects on the team's board
Average number of people who touched each item
Team velocity measured in points per sprint
Lead time, the elapsed days from when a request is made until it is delivered
questions.why: Lead time measures the full span from request to delivery, which is the question a product owner is asking about when a feature will land.

questions.prompt: A payroll support team of four finishes about 6 tickets a week. Its queue has grown from 12 open-and-started tickets to 24 over four weeks while throughput stayed at 6 a week. What should the team expect for average cycle time?
choices: Cycle time cannot be estimated without the team's velocity
Cycle time rises to about 4 weeks, because 24 divided by 6 is 4
Cycle time falls to 1 week, because a busier queue clears faster
Cycle time stays at 2 weeks, because throughput did not change
questions.why: With throughput flat, Little's Law says cycle time moves in step with WIP, so doubling WIP from 12 to 24 at 6 tickets a week doubles cycle time from 2 weeks to 4 weeks.

questions.prompt: A director asks a delivery team of five to raise its velocity from 30 to 40 points next quarter. What response best fits how the team should use this metric?
choices: Keep velocity as the team's own sprint planning tool, and ask what is blocking flow today rather than turning velocity into a goal
Adopt 40 points as the quarterly target and reward the team when it is reached
Compare the team's velocity with a neighbouring team to set a ranking
Ask the team to re-estimate every story weekly so the points rise steadily
questions.why: Velocity is a planning tool for one team, and making it a target inflates estimates and removes its meaning, so the useful response is to use it for planning and to ask flow questions instead.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who wants one dashboard for everyone how you would choose metrics for the team, the product owner, and leadership, and name one limit or tradeoff of the metric you would give executives.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not use one dashboard for everyone, because each audience asks a different question. The team needs day-to-day flow signals such as WIP, cycle time, and blocked items, so it can adjust its own work this week. The product owner needs predictability, so I would show lead time trends and throughput to forecast when features will land. Leadership needs outcome signals, such as how quickly value reaches customers and whether the work is worth doing. For executives I would give lead time, but its limit is that it hides why delays happen. A long lead time could come from a slow team, a waiting approval, or a poorly sized request, so it needs a team-level drill-down before anyone draws a conclusion. Every metric I show should be paired with a decision it is meant to inform.
rubricPoints: Matches each metric to a specific audience and the question that audience needs answered
Explains a flow metric such as cycle time, lead time, throughput, or WIP in plain terms
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as a metric hiding causes or being gamed
Connects the metric to an action or decision it should drive

suggested.rationale: An exam-style situation where the learner must choose metrics for a given audience and act on them adds the most to these definitions.

lessons.plain: This is about spotting the things that could slow a team down or derail its goal before they hit, and keeping a list of what is blocking work right now. An impediment is something already in the way that the team cannot clear alone. A risk is something that has not happened yet but might, and would hurt if it did. Ranking them by how likely and how costly they are tells you what to deal with first. The other half is learning from what went wrong: writing the lesson down as a specific change the team will actually use, so the same trouble does not return next month. Think of a ship's crew who check the weather before leaving port and also log every near-miss so the next voyage avoids the same rock.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has five open problems and time for only two this week. Before reading on, how would you decide which two to work on, and what would you write down so the team does not forget the other three?
lessons.teach:
An impediment is anything that is currently blocking or slowing the team and that the team cannot remove on its own, such as waiting for an approval or a shared test environment that is down. A risk is an uncertain event that may or may not happen; if it does, it changes the outcome. Each risk gets a rough probability (how likely it is) and an impact (how much it would cost, in days, money or quality). Multiplying the two gives exposure, a single number that lets you compare risks side by side. Exposure is a planning aid, not a precise forecast.

Why it works: a team cannot act on everything, so ranking by exposure points effort at the largest expected loss. A risk burndown chart plots total exposure over time. As mitigations are completed, the line should fall. If it stays flat, the mitigations are not working.

Worked example. A release has three risks. (a) The partner's API may change its format: probability 0.3, impact 8 days, exposure 2.4. (b) The only security reviewer is on leave: probability 0.5, impact 3 days, exposure 1.5. (c) The load-test environment is shared: probability 0.2, impact 10 days, exposure 2.0. Step 1: list each risk with a probability and impact. Step 2: multiply. Step 3: sort them, giving the partner API first (2.4), then the environment (2.0), then the reviewer (1.5). Step 4: give the top items an owner and a mitigation, such as an adapter layer that isolates the API change.

Common mistake: recording impediments in a log with no owner or date, so they age silently. Every impediment needs an owner and a next step.

Lessons learned only prevent recurrence when they become a specific change to practice, such as adding a contract test to the partner feed, and that change is checked at the next review. A note saying communication could be better changes nothing.

Consequence in a running system: an unowned dependency risk often surfaces as a failed deploy late in the iteration, just as an unreviewed config change causes an outage. An unowned risk that surfaces late costs far more than the same risk handled early.

questions.prompt: A logistics team lists four risks for a warehouse app release. Risk 1: the scanner firmware may change its label format, probability 0.4, impact 6 days, exposure 2.4. Risk 2: the only database administrator is covering two other projects, probability 0.5, impact 2 days, exposure 1.0. Risk 3: the carrier's sandbox may be unavailable, probability 0.2, impact 9 days, exposure 1.8. Done so far: each risk has a probability and impact, exposures are multiplied, and the list is sorted with the scanner firmware risk first. Not yet done: the top risk has no owner and no review date. Which action completes that missing step?
choices: Add a fifth risk about possible office internet outages to make the list more complete
Write a lessons-learned note saying the team should communicate better about firmware changes
Re-estimate every impact in weeks instead of days so the numbers look more precise
Assign a named owner and a next review date to the scanner firmware risk and record both in the log
questions.why: The top-ranked risk needs an owner and a next step with a date, because unowned items age silently, and the other choices do not give it either.

questions.prompt: A developer cannot start a task because the legal team has not yet signed a data-processing agreement, and the developer has no authority to sign it. Which label best describes this situation?
choices: A risk: it is an uncertain event that may or may not happen later in the project
An impediment: it is blocking work now and the team cannot remove it on its own
A lessons-learned item: it is a past event that should be reviewed at the next retrospective
An exposure: it is the probability multiplied by the impact of the delay
questions.why: The blocker exists now, is slowing the team, and is outside the team's control, which is the definition of an impediment.

questions.prompt: A team has three risks. Risk A has probability 0.6 and impact 2 days. Risk B has probability 0.1 and impact 15 days. Risk C has probability 0.3 and impact 4 days. Which risk should receive attention first, using exposure to rank them?
choices: Risk A, because it is the most likely to happen and so will cause the most trouble
Risk B, because its exposure of 1.5 is higher than the 1.2 for both A and C
Risk C, because its impact is a moderate middle value that balances the other two
All three should be treated equally because their exposures are close together
questions.why: Exposure is probability times impact: A gives 1.2, B gives 1.5, and C gives 1.2, so B ranks first.

questions.prompt: After a release slipped because a vendor changed its test endpoint without notice, the team wants a lesson-learned entry that will actually prevent the problem from happening again. Which entry best does this?
choices: The team will pay closer attention to dependencies from now on, and everyone will try harder to notice changes
A manager reminder that schedules matter and that vendor problems should be escalated quickly when they appear
Add an automated daily check of the vendor endpoint, and review whether the check caught any change at the next retrospective
The team agreed to communicate better with vendors and to be more careful about external dependencies in future work
questions.why: A lesson only prevents recurrence when it becomes a specific, checkable change to practice, and the automated check with a review date does that while the other entries do not.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which risk or impediment the team tackles first this sprint, and name one limit of the method you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would list each open impediment and risk, give each a rough probability and impact, and multiply them to get exposure. That ranks them, and the top items get an owner and a concrete next step that day. Impediments the team cannot clear alone go to whoever can remove them, with a date. The limit is that the probabilities are guesses, so the ranking is only as good as the team's honesty about them. I would revisit the scores at each review, and watch the burndown of total exposure to see whether the mitigations work. Lessons from anything that went wrong would become a specific practice change with an owner, checked at the next retrospective, so the same problem does not come back.
rubricPoints: Defines an impediment as a blocker the team cannot clear alone and a risk as an uncertain event
Explains ranking by exposure, meaning probability times impact, to focus effort
Notes that every item needs an owner and a next step rather than sitting in a log
Names a limit such as subjective probability estimates or the need to re-score
Explains that a lesson learned must become a specific, checked change in practice

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises risk ranking or lessons-learned capture, so explaining the reasoning back is the core skill for this objective.

lessons.plain: Waste in delivery means any effort that does not move a finished, useful result closer to a customer. Think of a kitchen where cooks spend half their time walking to a fridge, or where orders sit on a counter waiting for a second check. Agile teams first draw the whole path a piece of work travels, from idea to customer, and mark each step as either work that changes the product or work that only waits, repeats, or rechecks. Once the picture is clear, the team picks the biggest sources of waiting and removes those first, instead of trying to fix everything at once.
