lessons.guessPrompt: A team says every story is done in two weeks, but most stories sit idle for nine of those days. Before any teaching, which single change would you expect to shorten the real delivery time the most, and why?
lessons.teach:
Value-added work is any activity a customer would pay for, because it changes the product in a way they care about, such as writing the code that handles a new order type. Non-value-added work, often called waste in lean thinking, is everything else that still consumes time: waiting in a queue for review, rework caused by unclear requirements, handoffs where one person must re-explain context to another, and extra approvals. The first step is a value stream map, which is a visual of every step from the moment work is requested until a customer uses it. For each step you record how long the work actively takes and how long it sits waiting. The ratio of active time to total elapsed time is called flow efficiency, and in many teams it is far below half. Cycle time, the time from starting a piece of work to finishing it, is the number that customers feel.

Why this works: waiting is usually where the time goes, and queues grow whenever more work starts than finishes. Visualizing the path makes the waiting visible, so you can target it.

Worked example: a feature takes 2 days of coding, 1 day waiting for review, 3 days waiting for a test environment, and 1 day of testing. Active time is 3 days out of 7 elapsed, about 43 percent efficiency. The biggest waste is the 3-day environment wait, so the team reserves a shared environment slot first rather than tuning the review step.

Common mistake: optimizing the busiest person or the fastest step, such as making coding faster when coding is not the bottleneck. Speeding up a non-bottleneck changes nothing about delivery time.

Consequence: if waste sits unaddressed, every new story waits behind the same queue, and the team reports growing cycle times even though everyone is working hard.

questions.prompt: A marketing team publishes one blog post at a time. Drafting takes 2 days of active work. The draft then waits 5 days for legal review. Editing takes 1 day of active work. The edited post waits 2 days for a publishing slot. Publishing takes 0.5 day of active work. Active time totals 3.5 days and total elapsed time is 10.5 days, so flow efficiency is about 33 percent. Step to complete: identify the single largest waste in this flow and state which step the team should address first. The answer is the step with the longest wait, which is the legal review wait of 5 days.
choices: Remove the publishing step, because it is the smallest step in the flow
Reduce the drafting time, because drafting is the first step
Reduce the 5-day legal review wait, because it is the largest single waste
Speed up the editing step, because it has the largest active time
questions.why: Waste reduction targets the largest queue, and the 5-day legal review wait is larger than any active step or other wait in this flow.

questions.prompt: A support team handles refund requests. Which of these steps is value-added work according to the lean view of flow?
choices: Waiting in a queue for a manager to approve a batch of tickets
Redoing a refund calculation because the original request was unclear
Writing a new validation rule that stops duplicate refund requests from being paid
Having a second person sign off on a refund that the first person already checked
questions.why: Value-added work changes the product in a way the customer cares about, and only writing the new validation rule does that; the other three consume time without changing what the customer receives.

questions.prompt: A small team tracks one piece of work through its flow. It spends 2 days in active work and 6 days waiting, split into a 4-day wait for a design sign-off and a 2-day wait for a deployment window. Which action best follows the prioritization principle of waste reduction?
choices: Hire another developer to increase coding throughput
Target the 4-day design sign-off wait first, since it is the largest waste
Pair programmers so that active coding time is halved
Ask the team to work longer hours so stories finish sooner
questions.why: The principle is to find where the time goes, which is waiting, and address the largest waiting step first rather than speeding up active work that is not the main source of delay.

questions.prompt: A product team has steady coding speed, but its reported cycle time has grown for three months. Team members say they are all busy. Based on how queues form, what is the most likely cause?
choices: The team has taken on more value-added work, which by definition lengthens cycle time
The customer changed how they measure cycle time, so the numbers are not comparable
Work is starting faster than it finishes, so a queue builds in front of a waiting step and every new item waits behind it
Developers have become less skilled over the quarter, which slows every active step
questions.why: Queues grow whenever more work starts than finishes, and unaddressed queues make each new item wait longer even when everyone is working hard.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which waste to remove first after mapping a delivery flow, and name one limit or tradeoff of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first map the path a request takes from start to customer and record, for each step, the active work time and the waiting time. Then I would rank the waste by how many elapsed days it adds to the whole flow, not by how annoying it feels or how busy a person looks. The largest waiting queue usually sits at the bottleneck, so removing that delay shortens the entire flow. The tradeoff is that the map is only a snapshot. Work mix changes, so a queue that dominated last month may not be the constraint now, and the team needs to remap after changes. Also, some waste such as a single approval may be required by compliance, so I would confirm with the people involved before cutting it.
rubricPoints: Separates value-added active work from non-value-added waiting, rework and handoffs.
Maps the end-to-end flow so waiting time is visible, not just task time.
Prioritizes waste by its effect on total elapsed time, usually at the bottleneck.
Names a limit such as a stale map or a step that is required by policy.

suggested.rationale: A scenario where the learner traces a flow and chooses which waste to cut adds more than reading definitions, and no listed mission covers flow mapping directly.

lessons.plain: Continuous improvement means a team regularly looks at how its work is going, using numbers and feedback from people, picks one small change to try, and then checks whether that change actually made things better. It is a loop rather than a one-time fix: notice a problem, decide on a change, try it, check the result, then keep it or drop it. Many teams skip the last step, so they pile up changes nobody can say helped. The goal is to make improvement a habit that is tested, not a feeling or a fashion.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team decides in its retrospective to 'communicate better' and changes nothing else in how it works. Two sprints later, people say it feels better. What is the weakness in how the team knows whether the change worked, and what should it have measured before starting?
lessons.teach:
A retrospective is a regular team meeting, held at the end of each iteration, where the team looks back at how its work went and chooses what to change. A metric is a number tracked over time, such as how many days a work item takes from start to done, which is called cycle time. A baseline is the value of a metric before you change anything. An improvement experiment is a small, time-limited change with a stated expected result, so you can check it later. This approach works because a baseline gives you something to compare against, and small changes are easy to reverse if they do not help.

Worked example. A team's median cycle time is 9 days. In retrospective, members say work waits too long in review. Step 1: record the baseline of 9 days. Step 2: write the experiment: reviewers take two fixed review slots per day. Step 3: state the expectation: median cycle time falls below 6 days within three iterations. Step 4: after three iterations, the median is 5.5 days, and the defect count has not risen, so the team keeps the practice and records the result.

Common mistake: judging success by feeling, or by one unusually good sprint, or changing four things at once so nobody can tell which one helped.

Consequence: if a team credits a change for a drop that was really a quiet workload week, it keeps a practice that does nothing and spends effort on it every day.

An improvement is only proven when the team compares the same measure before and after its change.

questions.prompt: A support team at a regional bank measures the median time from ticket open to ticket close. Before any change it is 20 hours, which is the baseline. The team tries one experiment: a 15-minute daily triage of password-reset tickets, with the expectation that median open-to-close time falls below 15 hours within four weeks. After four weeks the median is 14 hours and the reopened-ticket count has not risen. The team now needs to decide whether the improvement is proven. What step is missing before that decision?
choices: How people felt about the triage at the retrospective
Compare the new median against the 20-hour baseline, both measured as open to close
The single best week of ticket closures after the change
Export every chart the ticketing tool can produce for the month
questions.why: An improvement is only proven when the same measure is compared before and after the change, so the 14-hour median must be set against the 20-hour open-to-close baseline.

questions.prompt: A team at a logistics firm counts 42 failed builds in a month before it changes anything. What is that count of 42 in the terms this course uses?
choices: A retrospective outcome
A cycle time
A baseline
An improvement experiment
questions.why: A baseline is the value of a metric before any change is made, and a count of failed builds taken before the change is exactly that.

questions.prompt: A product team changed four things in the same iteration and its median cycle time dropped from 12 days to 8 days. Which response best fits the idea that a change is only credited when it can be separated from the others?
choices: Keep all four, since the total drop shows they work together
Reverse all four, since any multi-change result is invalid
Credit the largest change and drop the rest
Test changes one at a time against the 12-day baseline
questions.why: Changing several things at once means no one can tell which one caused the drop, so each change should be tested separately against the original baseline.

questions.prompt: A retail software team has a median cycle time of 6 days. It runs a 10-minute daily blocker check as an experiment, expecting the median to fall below 5 days within two iterations. After two iterations the median is 5 days, but the defect count per release has risen from 3 to 9. What is the right call?
choices: Keep it, since the cycle time target was met
Do not keep it yet: speed improved but defects rose
Replace the baseline with last quarter's average
Keep it and ignore defects, since speed is the goal
questions.why: The target was met, but a rise in defects means the change has a side effect, so the improvement is not yet proven and should not be kept on the speed result alone.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined how our team decides whether a process change from the retrospective actually worked. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on our own team metrics to judge this.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before we change anything, we record a baseline on a metric tied to the problem we are fixing, such as cycle time or the number of items sent back from review. We write the change as a small experiment, with an expected result and a review date, usually after one to three iterations. At the review we compare the same metric against the baseline, and we also check a guardrail metric, such as defect count, to be sure the change did not hurt something else. Then we keep, adjust or drop the change and write the result down. One limit is that team metrics are noisy and small samples are easy to misread, so a change can look like it worked purely by chance or because workload dropped. We treat the result as evidence to discuss with the team, not as proof.
rubricPoints: Names a baseline measured before the change
Describes a small experiment with a stated expected result and review date
Checks a guardrail metric so one gain does not hide a loss elsewhere
Notes a limit such as noisy data, small samples or outside causes

suggested.rationale: Explaining how to judge a change against a baseline back to a teammate, including its limits, is the core skill here and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Actively engaging customers means keeping the people who will use the product close to the work. You find out what they really need, check each finished piece against a written list of what done well means, and let customers and builders talk directly rather than passing messages through a chain of middlemen. The idea is simple: the closer the feedback loop, the less time anyone spends building the wrong thing. Think of a bakery owner who lets regular customers taste the bread before it reaches the shelf.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has spent three sprints building a report that matches the written requirements document exactly, but the customer says it is not what they need. Where do you think the gap came from, and what one practice would have caught it earlier?
lessons.teach:
A customer need is the outcome a person is trying to achieve, which is often different from the request they write down. Acceptance criteria are the specific, testable conditions a deliverable must meet before anyone calls it finished. Validation is checking a finished piece of work against those criteria, with the customer or their representative, to confirm it does what it is for. Direct collaboration means the people who build and the people who use the product talk without intermediaries, so questions get answered the same day rather than after a week of email.

Why it works: a written request is a guess at a need, and building against a guess for weeks is expensive. Showing a working piece to the person who asked, while changes are still cheap, tests the guess early.

Worked example: a dispatcher asks for a faster route report. The team asks what faster means. She says she needs the route list by 07:00 with late stops flagged. The team writes three criteria: the list appears by 07:00 for every depot, each stop past its window is flagged, and the dispatcher can reorder stops. At the end of the sprint the team demonstrates the feature at her desk. Two criteria pass. The flag is wrong for stops with no window. She sees it in the room, and the fix takes an hour instead of a release cycle.

Common mistake: treating sign-off as a formality, where work is accepted without the customer ever seeing it, so the gap stays hidden until production.

In a running system, if feedback arrives only at release, a wrong assumption reaches dispatchers and the operations team learns of it from complaints. Putting acceptance criteria in front of a real user before the work is finished finds the mismatch while it is still cheap to fix.

questions.prompt: A clinic's scheduling team is building a reminder list for front-desk staff. The clinic manager writes: I need to call people who have not confirmed. The team asks what she needs the list for. She says she must finish confirmation calls before the 09:00 opening and record each call result on the list. The team writes three criteria: the list is ready by 08:30 each morning, every unconfirmed appointment for that day appears on it, and staff can mark a call as made. At the end of the sprint the team shows the feature in the team room using a screen recording only. The team then closes the item as done. What is the missing step?
choices: Move the item to the next sprint's backlog for reprioritisation
Ask the developers to add a fourth criterion about the colour of the flags
Wait a week for email feedback from the front-desk staff before deciding
Show the manager the list working on real appointments and check each criterion with her before accepting
questions.why: Validation means checking the finished work against the criteria with the customer or their representative, using real conditions, before it is accepted, and the team skipped that step.

questions.prompt: A logistics coordinator writes: I need the stock count to be more accurate. Which statement best captures the customer need, meaning the outcome she is trying to achieve?
choices: A newer stock screen with a barcode scanner attached to it
She can promise client delivery dates without recounting stock by hand
A testable rule that every count matches a physical check on the shelf
A count that is accurate, as the written request says
questions.why: A customer need is the outcome the person is trying to achieve, which here is being able to promise delivery dates without manual recounts, not the device or the wording of the request.

questions.prompt: A product owner who is also the development team's line manager reviews each sprint's work alone and records it as accepted. No customer sees the work. Which risk does this practice create?
choices: The gap between the written request and the real need stays hidden until users find it in production
The product owner cannot write useful meeting notes afterward
The team will need more story points to finish the next sprint
The sprint review runs longer than the team's calendar allows
questions.why: Treating sign-off as a formality hides mismatches until production, where fixes are expensive and users are the ones who find the problem.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team is writing acceptance criteria for a new picking app used by staff who walk aisles with handheld scanners. Which criterion is written in a testable way?
choices: Pickers say the app feels quick and easy to use during a typical shift
The screen layout looks modern and clean to the warehouse manager and her team leads
A pick list shows bin codes in aisle order, and a scan that does not match the list shows an error
The development team has tested the app thoroughly and feels confident about it
questions.why: A testable criterion states a specific condition that can be checked as met or not met, such as bin ordering and a visible error on a mismatched scan, whereas the other choices rely on opinion or vague confidence.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who thinks customer engagement just means a demo at the end of the sprint: what does validating against acceptance criteria add, and what is a limit or tradeoff of having customers in the room with the team?
lessons.modelAnswer: A demo at the end of a sprint shows work, but it does not prove the work meets what the customer needs. Acceptance criteria turn the need into testable conditions, and validating against them means checking each one with the customer, so a failing condition is found while changing it is cheap. Direct collaboration shortens the loop further, because questions get answered the same day. The tradeoff is time and focus: customers are busy, and frequent sessions can pull them away from their own work or make them feel asked to do the team's job. Some customers also ask for features that sound good in the room but serve few users. So the team needs a named customer representative with authority to decide, and it should weigh feedback against the wider user base rather than treating the loudest voice as the requirement.
rubricPoints: Acceptance criteria are specific, testable conditions that define finished, checked with the customer
Validation catches gaps between the written request and the real need while change is cheap
Direct customer-team contact shortens the feedback loop compared with intermediaries
Tradeoffs include customer time, focus, and the risk of over-weighting one voice

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises customer-facing judgement, so explaining the idea to a teammate is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Flow optimization means getting finished work out the door steadily, instead of having many half-finished items stuck in the middle. The main lever is a work-in-progress limit: a hard cap on how many items can be active at once, in a stage or across the team. It sounds backwards, since starting more seems productive, but when people juggle too much, every item waits longer and takes longer to finish. Shielding the team means protecting that focus from outside interruptions, such as urgent side requests, so the cap actually holds. Teams then watch a few flow measures to see whether their changes help. The same idea works for one team or for a group of teams.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team of four has ten items started and none finished for two weeks, and their manager asks them to start two more items to speed things up. Would you agree with the manager, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Work in progress (WIP) is the number of items that have been started but not yet finished. A WIP limit is a cap you set on that number. It can apply to a column on a board, to one person, to a whole team, or across several teams in a portfolio. Limits can be applied at every level, so the same logic holds at each one.

Why it works: each active item competes for the same attention. When people hold five items at once, they switch constantly, and little gets closed. Little's Law, a result from queueing theory, ties the numbers together. Average cycle time (the time from starting one item to finishing it) equals average WIP divided by average throughput (items finished per time period). If throughput stays the same, lowering WIP directly lowers cycle time.

Worked example: a team finishes 2 stories per week, and with no limit about 8 stories are in progress on average. Cycle time is 8 divided by 2, which is 4 weeks. The team sets a WIP limit of 4. Throughput stays at 2 per week, so cycle time becomes 4 divided by 2, which is 2 weeks. Step by step: count the active items, compare the count to the cap, and pull no new work until one item finishes.

Shielding the team means keeping interruptions out of that capped set. A new urgent request should either wait, replace an existing item, or be allowed past the limit with the cost stated openly. Otherwise the limit is decorative.

Common mistake: setting a limit and then ignoring it the moment a deadline appears, or counting only the developers' work while hidden tasks pile up in a separate queue nobody measures.

Consequence in a running system: when work starts faster than it finishes, queues grow, waiting time rises, and everyone looks busy while delivery slows.

questions.prompt: A finance reconciliation team of 5 people closes 6 monthly reports per week on average. Before any limit, about 18 reports are open at once. Step 1, already done: cycle time before the limit is 18 divided by 6, which is 3 weeks. Step 2, already done: the team caps open reports at 9 and throughput stays at 6 per week. Missing step: using Little's Law, what is the new average cycle time?
choices: 1.5 weeks, because the new WIP of 9 divided by throughput of 6 gives the cycle time
3 weeks, because throughput is unchanged so cycle time cannot change
9 weeks, because the cap is subtracted from the old WIP
0.67 weeks, because the throughput is divided by the cap
questions.why: Little's Law says cycle time equals average WIP divided by throughput, so 9 divided by 6 gives 1.5 weeks.

questions.prompt: A platform team has 7 items in progress and finishes 3.5 items per week on average. Using Little's Law, what is the average cycle time?
choices: 2 weeks
3.5 weeks
7 weeks
0.5 weeks
questions.why: Cycle time equals average WIP divided by throughput, so 7 divided by 3.5 is 2 weeks.

questions.prompt: A product group caps each developer at 2 items on the board. Mid-sprint, a senior executive sends an urgent request that is handled by one developer directly, outside the board, and the developer's board count stays at 2. What is the main flaw in this arrangement?
choices: The cap should have been set at 4 items per developer to absorb urgent work
The urgent request is hidden work, so the limit no longer reflects the load and the cost of the interruption is not visible
Executives should never send requests mid-sprint, so the request itself is the only problem
The developer should have finished one item first, which would have made the board count drop to 1
questions.why: Interruptions that bypass the capped set make the limit decorative because real load is hidden and the trade-off is never stated.

questions.prompt: A team measures its WIP and cycle time only for developers' coding tasks. Testing is handled by a separate group with a queue of 15 tickets that nobody counts. Which change best restores accurate flow measurement?
choices: Count the testing queue as part of the team's WIP and measure cycle time from start to finish across the whole path
Ask the testing group to report their queue size once a quarter
Ignore the testing queue, since it belongs to another group and is outside the team's control
Lower the developers' WIP cap to make room for the testing queue
questions.why: Hidden queues distort WIP and cycle time, so the measurement must cover the full path from starting work to finishing it, including the testing queue.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who believes a higher WIP limit always means more output why a team might lower its WIP limit, and name one limit or tradeoff of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A higher WIP limit does not guarantee more output, because active items share the same people and attention. Once there are more items than the team can focus on, each one waits longer, so cycle time grows while throughput stays roughly flat. Little's Law shows the relationship: cycle time equals WIP divided by throughput. If we lower WIP and keep throughput the same, items finish sooner and feedback arrives faster. The tradeoff is that a low limit can leave people idle when an item is blocked, and it can create friction when a stakeholder expects new work to start immediately. That is why the limit has to be paired with shielding the team from interruptions and with a clear rule for what happens when someone must exceed it.
rubricPoints: Defines WIP as started but unfinished items and explains that a limit caps it
Connects lower WIP to shorter cycle time using Little's Law or an equivalent reasoning
Notes that interruptions must be shielded or the limit is ineffective
Names a real tradeoff, such as idle capacity when blocked or stakeholder pressure

suggested.rationale: Explaining the WIP and cycle time relationship to a teammate, with its tradeoffs, is the core skill here and no listed mission or planned engine covers flow metrics directly.

scenarios.title: Parcel Routing App: An Unclear Problem and a Quiet Developer
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Parcels Ltd is a fictional regional courier company. Its product team of seven people is building a mobile app that drivers use to choose their delivery order. Two months ago the team was told to 'fix late deliveries'. Nobody agrees on the cause. Some people blame the app, some blame depot staffing, and some believe customers give wrong addresses. Operations stakeholders want a finished feature by next quarter, but the team has never shown them a working version. In the daily stand-up, the developer Priya noticed that route suggestions fail whenever a depot changes its opening hours. She has not raised it, because the last time she reported a bug, her manager asked why she had not caught it earlier. You are the agile-minded project manager for this team. Answer the three sub-tasks below. 1. Classify the late-delivery problem using the Cynefin framework (a sense-making model that sorts situations into domains such as clear, complicated, complex and chaotic, based on how clearly cause and effect can be linked) and name the agile practice that fits that domain. 2. Propose a thin increment (the smallest working slice of a product that you can put in front of real users to test one assumption) and explain how you would get stakeholder feedback from it within two weeks. 3. Describe one psychological-safety move you would make with Priya and the team so that impediments like the opening-hours problem are raised early.
subParts: Classify complexity and choose a fitting practice
Propose a thin increment and fast stakeholder feedback
modelAnswer: Cynefin sorts problems by how clearly cause and effect can be linked. In clear problems the answer is obvious, in complicated problems experts can analyse the cause, and in complex problems cause and effect only become visible in hindsight because many interacting parts influence each other. In chaotic problems, immediate action is needed to stop harm. Late deliveries involve drivers, depots, customers and the app all interacting, with several competing causes, so this sits in the complex domain. The fitting practice is to run small safe-to-fail experiments, observe the results, and respond, rather than writing a full up-front specification or a fixed plan. The common mistake is treating it as complicated and commissioning one detailed root-cause study that assumes a single answer. The consequence is months spent on a plan built on a guessed cause, while the real driver, the opening-hours changes, goes unnoticed.

A thin increment is the smallest working slice that tests one assumption with real users. For example, the team could release only the route ordering for one depot, including a check against opening hours, to the two drivers who volunteered. The team picks one assumption to test, builds that slice within one sprint, puts it in front of real users, and then shows the working slice to operations stakeholders in a short review. Within two weeks the team has measured data, such as late deliveries at that depot compared with others, plus direct stakeholder feedback that can reshape the backlog. The common mistake is building the whole feature first and planning to demonstrate it later. The consequence is that feedback arrives months late, when changes are expensive and the team has little room to adapt.

Psychological safety means people believe they can raise problems, mistakes or disagreements without being punished or embarrassed. A no-blame move keeps the focus on the process rather than the person. For example, the manager could thank Priya for the opening-hours report and say that exactly this kind of issue should be raised early. She could then add the issue to a visible impediment board that everyone can see, and ask the whole team which other issues they have been holding back. The common mistake is publicly praising the report while privately still asking why it was not caught earlier. The consequence is that people go quiet, impediments stay hidden, and the team discovers problems late, when they are harder and more costly to fix.

scenarios.title: Dispatch App Team: Conflict, Failed Releases, and a Drifting Goal
scenarios.scenario:
Northgate Freight is a fictional mid-sized trucking company. Its internal software team builds a dispatch app that tells drivers which load to pick up next. You have just become the team's agile project manager, a role that focuses on helping the team work well together and deliver value, not on assigning tasks to individuals. The team has seven people: a product owner (the person who decides what gets built and in what order), five developers, and a tester.

Three problems have surfaced in the last month. First, two senior developers, Dana and Marcus, have stopped speaking directly. In the last sprint review, Dana rejected Marcus's pull request (a proposed code change that others must approve before it merges) with a single line, and Marcus replied in the team chat that he would no longer take review requests from her. Other developers now route their work around the two of them, and the tester says people are avoiding standup. Second, the last four production releases each broke the driver login screen and had to be rolled back (undone and restored to the previous working version). Nobody has yet established why. Third, the product owner recently said in a meeting that the app's main goal is 'to get the new feature out by March,' while the company's stated goal is to cut empty return trips by a fifth. Several developers now say they do not know which goal matters more.

In one short paragraph, explain that 'conflict level' means how far a disagreement reaches (inside one person, between two people, within the team, or between groups), and that a root cause is the underlying reason a problem keeps happening, not the visible symptom. Then complete these sub-tasks:

1. Decide the level of the Dana and Marcus conflict and name its most likely root cause. Then say which collaborative approach you would use first, and why it fits this level.

2. Use root-cause analysis on the four failed releases. Explain how you would group possible causes using an Ishikawa diagram (a fishbone diagram, a chart that sorts candidate causes into branches such as people, process, tools, and environment), and name the single cause you would test first.

3. The team recently finished a similar login-related release fix for a different internal app, built by another group at Northgate. Explain how you would capture the lessons from this initiative and bring the relevant knowledge into the dispatch team's work, and say how you would restate the shared purpose so that the feature date and the empty-mile goal are no longer in competition.
subParts: Conflict level and first collaborative move
Root cause of the failed releases
Sharing lessons and restating the shared purpose
modelAnswer: This is an interpersonal conflict, meaning a disagreement between two people, though it is already affecting the wider team because others are routing around it. The most likely root cause is not the single rejected pull request but an unresolved trust problem: the two developers have no agreed way to disagree about code, so a review comment became a personal slight. The first collaborative move is a private, facilitated conversation between Dana, Marcus, and you, focused on shared interests such as release quality and the team's working agreement on reviews, not on who was right. Starting privately fits an interpersonal level better than a team retrospective, because public discussion first would raise the stakes for both. After that, the team can agree on written review guidelines so future disagreements stay about the code.

Create an Ishikawa diagram with a central problem statement, 'login screen breaks after release,' and branches for people, process, tools, and environment. Under process you might list a missing automated login test before release. Under environment you might list that the staging server differs from production. Under tools you might list a deployment script that copies a configuration file. Under people you might list reviewers who are overloaded. Then ask 'why' repeatedly on the strongest branch to reach the root, for example: why did the login break? Because a configuration file differed between staging and production. Why? Because the deployment script copies staging settings without checking. The single cause to test first is that the deployment script copies configuration without validation, because it appears in all four failed releases and is cheap to test in a controlled run before changing anything else.

Capture lessons by running a short, blame-free review of the other group's login fix, recording what went wrong, what worked, and what to do differently in a shared lessons-learned note that both teams can find. Bring the knowledge into the dispatch team by inviting that group to a short session where they explain their configuration checks, then adding one of those checks to the team's definition of done (the shared checklist a feature must meet before it counts as finished). For the shared purpose, restate the goal as one sentence linking the two: the March feature exists to reduce empty return trips, so each release is judged by whether it moves that outcome without breaking drivers' login. Repeat this framing at every sprint review and invite the product owner to confirm it, so the team hears the 'why' as consistently as the date.

scenarios.title: Returns Tracking Feature at Harbor Crate Co.
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Crate Co. is a fictional online retailer of kitchen goods. Its product owner, Dana, manages the backlog, which is the ordered list of work items the team may build, with the most valuable items at the top. Dana's top item is a single large entry called 'Customers can return items online.' It is too big to finish in one iteration, which is a fixed time box of about two weeks in the team's process. The team uses a Kanban board, a visual board with one column per stage of work such as To Do, In Progress, Testing and Done, and a work-in-progress limit, which is a cap on how many items may sit in one column at once. The team has also been asked to show that the feature is worth shipping, not just that it was built. Dana's manager wants the first increment, meaning the first usable slice of the feature that can be released and tested, to reduce return-related phone calls by 30 percent within three months. Compliance staff also require that refunds to card payments follow the payment provider's rules and that return labels never expose a customer's full address on the printed label. Complete the following three tasks. 1. Explain how Dana and the team should break down the large return item and size the resulting pieces together, and say why sizing as a group matters here. 2. Choose one work-visualization approach for the team's board, describe what the team should be taught about it, and state how the board's data must be kept current to remain useful. 3. Define what 'value' means for this increment, including the success criteria for sustainability, security and compliance, and explain how the team confirms after release whether the targeted 30 percent reduction in calls was actually achieved.
subParts: Decompose and size the return item
Choose and teach the visualization approach
Define value and confirm the targeted result
modelAnswer: Dana should split the large item into smaller items, each a thin, end-to-end slice that delivers something a customer or staff member can use, rather than splitting it by technical layer such as database first and screens later. For example, the first slice could let a customer start a return for one order that was delivered within 30 days and print a label, with no refunds or exchanges yet. Later slices can add refunds, exchanges and the compliance rules. The team then sizes each piece together, often by relative sizing, meaning comparing each item to a reference item and assigning a rough size such as small, medium or large, or using a planning-poker game where each member privately picks a card and the group discusses differences until they agree. Sizing collectively matters because people who will build the work hear different assumptions, such as which payment provider rules apply, and those hidden assumptions surface before commitment. Common mistake: Dana sizes the big item alone and hands it to the team, which hides risk until mid-sprint. Consequence: a large unsized item may be partly built and stuck in the Testing column, blocking the release of anything usable.

The team should adopt a Kanban board with clearly labelled columns for each stage of work and an explicit work-in-progress limit on the In Progress and Testing columns, for example no more than three items in progress at once. The approach is valuable because it makes bottlenecks visible: a pile-up in Testing shows where work is waiting. The team should be taught what each column means, the rule that an item moves right only when its exit criteria are met, why the limit exists (starting too much work slows every item down), and how to read the board during a daily check-in by asking what is blocked and what is nearly done. The board's data must be kept current by updating an item's column the moment its status changes, not in a batch at the end of the day, and by recording blockers as soon as they occur. Common mistake: the board is updated only before a review meeting, so it shows a rosy picture while real items sit stalled. Consequence: managers make decisions from stale data, such as adding people to a stage that is not the real constraint.

Value here means a measurable benefit to the business and to customers, not simply that the code was delivered. For this increment, success criteria should include the target of reducing return-related phone calls by 30 percent within three months of release, measured by comparing the weekly call count from a baseline period before release with the counts afterward. Sustainability means the feature must be maintainable, for example by keeping automated tests in place and avoiding shortcuts that will slow future changes. Security means return labels must never show a customer's full address, and access to return records must be restricted to authorized staff. Compliance means refunds to card payments must follow the payment provider's rules, which should be checked against a written checklist before release. After release, the team confirms the result by pulling the call-volume data from the baseline and post-release periods, comparing the two, and recording whether the 30 percent target was met, along with the compliance checklist sign-off and a security review of the label output. If the target is missed, the team reports the gap and adjusts the next increment rather than declaring success. Common mistake: counting features shipped as proof of value. Consequence: the business believes the problem is solved while calls continue to rise, and the team has no evidence to guide the next increment.

scenarios.title: Returns Portal Flow and Feedback Reset at Harbor Lane Furniture
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lane Furniture is a fictional online retailer. Its six-person team is building a returns portal, a web feature that lets customers start a return and get a refund. Stakeholders have seen nothing until a quarterly review, and the team board shows three problems. Nine items are In Progress across three people, fourteen items sit in a 'Waiting for review' column for an average of four days each, and a payment-provider security certificate renewal has been flagged as a blocker with no named owner. Mei, the product owner, asks you, the new project manager, to act within two weeks. Complete these tasks: 1. Propose how the team will deliver small increments and collect stakeholder feedback on a regular cadence, and state what the first increment contains. 2. Trace the flow from 'Ready' to 'Done' on the board, label each step as value-added or non-value-added, choose the one waste to reduce first, and set a work-in-progress limit for the step that is the constraint. 3. Describe how you would record the certificate renewal in the impediment and risk list, prioritize it against other items, and capture a lesson learned so it does not recur.
subParts: Early feedback cadence and first increment
Flow map, waste choice, and WIP limit
modelAnswer: An increment is a small, usable slice of the product that can be shown to someone and tested, rather than a full feature delivered at the end. I would propose a two-week sprint review where the team demonstrates working software to Mei plus invited people from customer support and finance, and a short mid-sprint check where the support lead tries a clickable prototype. The first increment would be only the start-a-return form with one return reason and an email confirmation, released to a small test group. Feedback would be written down, tagged by theme such as wording, reason codes, or confusing steps, and reviewed at the next planning session. Worked example: on Tuesday of week one the team shows the prototype, the support lead says the return reason list does not match what customers actually ask about, and the team changes the list before any backend code is built. That change costs an hour instead of a rebuild. The common mistake is waiting for the quarterly review, so every correction arrives months after the work was done. The consequence is that the business may end up with a full returns flow it does not need, paid for by the team's effort.

Value-added work is any step that changes the product in a way a customer or stakeholder would pay for, such as writing the return form code. Non-value-added work does not change the product, and waiting is the clearest example. A flow map is a simple left-to-right picture of every state an item passes through, and I would walk it step by step: Ready, In Progress, Waiting for review, Testing, Done. Building and testing are value-added. The 'Waiting for review' column is non-value-added waste, because items sit idle while the product does not change. Fourteen items waiting four days each is the biggest contributor to cycle time, which is the elapsed time from start to Done, so I would reduce that waste first. A work-in-progress (WIP) limit is a cap on how many items may be started but not finished in a given state. I would set the review column limit at three, so new reviews must wait until a slot clears, and set a team-wide In Progress limit of six, which is two per person instead of the current three. The common mistake is setting the limit but letting people start new work anyway, which keeps the queue growing. The consequence is that cycle time will not drop, so I would check it weekly and adjust the limit if the queue stops shrinking.

An impediment is anything blocking the team's work right now, and a risk is an event that might happen later and affect the work. The certificate renewal is both: it blocks release readiness today and could cause refund failures if it lapses. I would record it in the impediment and risk list with a named owner, here the operations lead, and a date set three weeks before the expiry. To prioritize, I would weigh how likely it is and how much damage it would cause; with a fixed expiry date, a release that depends on it, and refunds that would fail in production, it ranks above low-impact items and gets a response this week. The response is to have operations confirm the renewal date and a checkpoint in the next two stand-ups. After the renewal is complete, I would hold a short lessons-learned review. The finding would be that nobody owned the renewal date and no reminder existed. The recurrence fix is to add certificate and license expiry dates to the team board with an owner and a check at each sprint review, and to record the fix in the lessons-learned log so the next renewal is tracked. The common mistake is labeling it an operations problem and not tracking it, which means the team learns about the expiry only when payments fail.
